note: Kar Narpathu 12: the dark clouds, like oiled elephants, rise on the right every day (ஏரும் வலம்), a sign beyond doubt. Ainthinai Aimpathu 1 ends on the same omen, வலனேருங் கார், after giving the cloud the colour of Mal, the spear of Murugan and the garland of Shiva.
teaches: The rightward rise is a fixed reassurance in the mullai venba, and holding the two together shows the Ainthinai poet strengthening a plain omen by assembling three gods' emblems around it, where Kar Narpathu leans on its daily regularity.

note: Kar Narpathu 1 makes the rainbow the garland on the chest of sea-coloured Mal; Ainthinai Aimpathu 1 gives Mal the cloud's dark body and gives the garland to Shiva as the konrai.
teaches: Both opening verses of the mullai collections divine the storm, but they share it out differently, so the god of the mullai was a ready frame that each poet filled by choosing which part of the sky belongs to which god.

note: Kar Narpathu 4: the friend calls the season, with peacocks and konrai, the medicine for the heroine's wasting pallor. Ainthinai Aimpathu 2: with the peacock calling and the rain cloud low, every sight of the sky turns the heroine's shoulders yellow. On a plain reading the same season cures the pallor and causes it.
teaches: Set side by side the friend's argument and the heroine's experience disagree about the same sky, which shows that the season-as-proof consolation works only from outside, while to the waiting woman the season itself is the illness.

note: Natrinai 69: if the evening came like this in the land where he went for work, he could not hold to his resolve. Ainthinai Aimpathu 3: is there not this rain in the land where our man went?
teaches: The pair shows a single argument of the waiting wife, that the season must reach him too and would bring him home, carried from evening in the long poem to the rain in the venba, where its failure becomes the sharper doubt whether the rain is in his land at all.

note: Kural 1224: when the lover is absent, evening comes like enemies to a killing ground. Ainthinai Aimpathu 6: evening, sweet with the bee at the jasmine for those who have company, comes and saws those who have no one.
teaches: Both women make evening a killer, but the venba adds that the same hour is sweet to the companioned, so it locates the couplet's hostility in the absence and not in evening itself, which the couplet's 'when the lover is absent' only implies.

note: Kural 1228: the herdsman's flute, envoy of the burning evening, is a weapon that kills. Ainthinai Aimpathu 7: at red evening the herdsman's fine little flute, played in joy once the cattle have fed, is to her like a spear thrown.
teaches: The couplet states that the flute is a deadly weapon, and the venba supplies the scene that explains it: the herdsman plays for joy at his own day's return, so the weapon is someone else's homecoming.

note: Akananuru 74: the heroine could hold firm on her friend's comfort if the hard-mouthed small flute (வல்வாய் சிறுகுழல்) of the unlettered herdsmen did not torment her in the evening. Ainthinai Aimpathu 7 calls the same small flute fine (சீர்சால் சிறுகுழல்) and its player glad, yet it strikes her like a spear.
teaches: One heroine blames the flute's harsh mouth and the other concedes its sweetness, so together they show the evening flute's pain moving from the instrument to the hearer, which is why the venba needs the simile of the spear.

note: Kar Narpathu 18: the forest, dull like the body of a poor man, has put forth beauty like a rich man's mind. Ainthinai Aimpathu 8: the valli, dull like the body of the parted, has grown lovely like the body of the united.
teaches: Both measure the revived plant by a human state, but Kar Narpathu uses poverty and wealth, the motive of his journey, and Ainthinai uses parting and union, its outcome, so the same simile can point either to why he left or to what she awaits.

note: Kar Narpathu 14: the friend is sure he will come quickly, since the cool rain cloud laughs softly as the jasmine shows its bright teeth. Ainthinai Aimpathu 9: he will come; the jasmine has opened its buds, having heard the secret of the new rain.
teaches: In both the friend's proof is the budding jasmine, but one reads it as the season's laughter and the other as the season's whispered secret already received, so the same flower serves as a public sign in one and as private knowledge in the other.

note: Natrinai 142: returning, the man tells his charioteer of the young woman of mullai-fitting chastity who rejoices when a guest comes even at night. Ainthinai Aimpathu 10: returning, he tells the charioteer to hurry to see her who stands with the bolt of her chastity drawn shut, hand to cheek.
teaches: The same speaker on the same road imagines the wife's chastity as an open door to guests in one poem and as a shut bolt in the other, so the pair shows karpu as both the household's hospitality and its closing against the world while the husband is away.

note: Natrinai 259: the friendship made with the hill lord in the millet field, chasing parrots and bathing in the falls by the vengai slope, now looks hard to keep because the millet heads have ripened dry. Ainthinai Aimpathu 11: the few days in the vengai grove of the millet field have gone, sweet because no one gave orders.
teaches: Natrinai gives the crop's ripening as the reason the meetings end and Ainthinai names what made them possible, the absence of anyone to command the girls, so together they show the secret love as lent by the harvest calendar and taken back by it.

note: In Akananuru 38 the friend imagines the hill man finding the swing, the pool and the reaped field empty, and regrets that she forgot to tell him 'the high hill crowned with that white waterfall is our village'. Ainthinai Aimpathu 12 is that telling: the guarding is over, and this village by the clean waterfall is our place.
teaches: The longer poem shows the cost of not telling him where the house is when the field closes, and the quatrain makes the telling itself, so the pair shows pointing out the village by its waterfall as the friend's expected move at harvest, the step that turns field meetings toward the house.

note: In Natrinai 213 the man asks the girls which is the small rock-fenced village near the roaring falls, and whether the guarding of the millet is theirs too. In Ainthinai Aimpathu 12 the friend says their guarding of the millet is over and this village by the waterfall is their place.
teaches: The man's question and the friend's answer use the same two markers, the waterfall village and the guarding of the millet, which shows the exchange as a set dialogue of kurinji courtship in which the friend's answer comes only when the guarding has ended.

note: Akananuru 388: a young hunter with a hound comes to the millet platform asking whether a wounded tusker has passed through their field. Ainthinai Aimpathu 14: he came like those who ask after a beast, but there is something else he means to ask.
teaches: Akananuru stages the hunter's question in full while Ainthinai compresses it into a simile, 'like those who ask after a beast', which shows that the asking-after-game approach was a recognised pretext the girls themselves could name and see through.
audit_text_issue: line 2 வினைவாய்த்து hard to construe

note: Natrinai 44: the man remembers the girl after she bathed in the falls with her companions, her large eyes reddened by the beating water. Ainthinai Aimpathu 15: the friend says the girl's red-lined eyes reddened because they bathed in the leaping falls after plucking vengai.
teaches: The eyes reddened by the waterfall are a cherished sight for the lover in Natrinai and an explanation offered to others in Ainthinai, so the same bath serves both the love and its concealment, which is why it is safe for the friend to name.

note: Akananuru 308: a tusker worn from fighting a tiger, its long wound unwashed, marks the hill of a man who comes by night; the friend asks him to come by day. Ainthinai Aimpathu 16: an elephant that escaped the tiger shrinks at every footfall on the path, and the girl cannot sleep remembering that path.
teaches: In Akananuru the tiger-wounded elephant only marks the hill while the friend argues for day visits, whereas Ainthinai carries the beast's after-fear onto the path itself and into the girl's sleepless eyes, showing how the same hill emblem can move from scenery to the measure of a lover's dread.

note: Natrinai 151: even if the girl's forehead pales and her shoulders grow thin, may the hill lord not come by night. Ainthinai Aimpathu 17: because he comes without fail, the girl, afraid for him, loses her bloom and wastes away.
teaches: Natrinai offers her wasting as the lesser harm to be borne so that he stays away at night, but Ainthinai shows the night visits themselves causing the wasting through fear, so neither his coming nor his staying away spares her and only marriage can.

note: Natrinai 306: the millet is being reaped and the hill girl sent home; how will he come now to see her? Ainthinai Aimpathu 18: not even the parrots come to the millet field now; do not forget your bond with her.
teaches: Natrinai states the practical loss at harvest, no place left to meet, and Ainthinai names the risk behind it, that like the parrots he may stop coming once the field is empty, so the pair shows the end of the guarding feared as a test of his memory as well as of access.

note: In Natrinai 104 the girl asks whether anyone but her thinks of the narrow midnight path he takes while thunder strikes and floods block the way. In Ainthinai Aimpathu 19 the friend, picturing him swimming the falls at midnight, says her heart asks what will become of the girl.
teaches: The girl fears the night path for the man, and the friend fears it for the girl who would not survive his harm, so the pair shows the danger of the night meeting passing through two hearts, with the friend's fear one step removed and therefore usable as an argument for marriage.

note: In Akananuru 388 the old velan says 'my lord's seizure brought this sickness; I know the cure', and the girl mocks him. In Ainthinai Aimpathu 20 the velan, not knowing that the hill man took her nature, says a spirit has seized her and sheds the kid's blood.
teaches: Akananuru lets the velan claim knowledge of the cure and Ainthinai calls him plainly the one who does not know, so together they show the veri rite built around the diviner's ignorance, with the girl's secret as the one thing his craft cannot read.

note: Both wives turn away the bard over the husband's வாய்மொழி: Akananuru 146 pities the woman who will trust that deceiver's word as she once did; Ainthinai Aimpathu 21 says the bard who asks her to trust it is hawking needles in the smiths' street.
teaches: Akananuru 146 shows the wife as a past victim of the man's word, and 21 shows why that history makes the bard's pleading absurd: she is the one market where his word cannot be sold.

note: Natrinai 200 has the friend warn the town's women against the bard's lie-wrapped crooked words; Ainthinai Aimpathu 21 treats his pleading not as dangerous but as pointless.
teaches: The two refusals name two faults in the go-between, falsehood that endangers others and futility before the wife who already knows, so the refusal of the bard had both a public and a private argument.

note: In Akananuru 56 the wife tells the bard who blundered into her house 'இம்மனை அன்று; அஃது உம்மனை'; in Ainthinai Aimpathu 22 she tells him 'நெறிஅதுகாண் எங்கையர் இற்கு'.
teaches: The same retort appears as a told comic incident in Akananuru and as a direct taunt in the four-line venba, which shows that pointing the bard to the other house was a fixed refusal move the later poet could use bare, without the story.

note: Kural 785: shared feeling alone, without meeting or acquaintance, gives the claim of friendship. Ainthinai Aimpathu 23: the bond of those who know needs no bard to plead for the man's grace.
teaches: The wife turns the Kural's rule about friendship into an argument against intercession in marriage: if feeling alone makes the bond, then the presence of a go-between is itself proof that the feeling is gone.

note: In Kuruntokai 376 the man says his beloved is cool like Pothiyil sandal in summer and warm like a lotus heart in the cold; in Ainthinai Aimpathu 24 the wife says her shoulders were once sandal paste to him and are now hotter than caustic.
teaches: The lover's praise of a body that tempers every season is answered by the wife's claim that the same body's heat follows his conduct, not the weather, so the courtship image is shown to depend on fidelity.

note: In Kalittokai 81 the son's prattle is praised as 'நோய் நாம் தணிக்கும் மருந்து', the medicine that eases our illness; in Ainthinai Aimpathu 25 the pain of longing for the man's chest is met by the son's மழலைவாய் கட்டுரை.
teaches: Both make the child's prattle the cure for the wife's love-sickness in a marutham quarrel, and Kalittokai's longer scene shows what the venba compresses: the boy repeats words learned in the street, so his chatter can carry the father back into the house.

note: Kural 66: only those who have not heard their children's prattle (மழலைச்சொல்) call the flute and lute sweet. Ainthinai Aimpathu 25: the son's மழலைவாய் talk eases the pain of longing for the husband.
teaches: The Kural ranks prattle above music as a pleasure; the venba gives it a harder task, standing in for an absent husband's embrace, so the general praise of children is tested in the one place it might fail.

note: In Akananuru 66 the husband, dressed for a new wedding, stops his chariot when his son runs to him and gives the wedding up; in Ainthinai Aimpathu 26, as the drums of his new wedding sound, the little one who goes after his chariot comes to grief. On the reading of இவன் as the son, the appeal that succeeds in one fails in the other.
teaches: Akananuru 66 presents the son as the force that turns a husband back from another marriage, and 26 shows the same scene with the opposite outcome, so the son's claim emerges as a hope the wives hold rather than a rule the poems guarantee.

note: Akananuru 66: seeing the son run to him, the man cries 'நெடுந்தேர் தாங்குமதி, வலவ!' and climbs down. Ainthinai Aimpathu 28: the son stands yearning, the man sees him and drives the chariot on without a look.
teaches: Set side by side the two chariots mark the test of a straying husband as whether he stops for his child, and 28 makes the wife's hardening a verdict on his failing that test rather than on his other women.

note: Kural 1309: sulking, like water in the shade, is sweet only with those who love. Ainthinai Aimpathu 27: the faded wife asks whether she is still one the man would sulk at.
teaches: The Kural's rule that a quarrel belongs inside love lets the wife read the man's absence of pulavi as the absence of love, so the venba shows the rule used as evidence by someone on the losing side.

note: Kural 1308: what use is suffering when there is no lover who knows we suffer? Ainthinai Aimpathu 29: she would refuse his embrace, but he has no thought of her refusal, so she will serve him.
teaches: Both say a protest needs a lover who registers it, and the venba draws the practical end the couplet stops short of: with no such lover, the wife abandons oodal and goes back to service.

note: Kural 1330: sulking is love's pleasure, and its pleasure is to embrace after it. Ainthinai Aimpathu 30: even while sulking, union with the man's fragrant body is sweet, like the south wind in the cold season.
teaches: The Kural places the embrace after the sulk, while the wife finds it sweet during the sulk itself, so the venba collapses the Kural's sequence and shows desire overriding the quarrel instead of crowning it.

note: Akananuru 99: the man leading the eloping girl bids her admire a forest strewn with murukku buds like the gripping claws of the striped tiger (கோள்உகிர் அன்ன). Aimpathu 31 uses the same simile, murukku buds like a tiger's blood-dyed claws, for the spring that breaks the waiting woman's heart.
teaches: Aimpathu 31 says outright that this season gives joy only to those who are together (எதிருநர்க்கு இன்பம்), and Akananuru 99 is that joy spoken by a man walking beside his girl, so the pair shows one flowering read as delight or as wound according to whether the lovers are together.

note: Kuruntokai 37: the friend tells the heroine that the road he took is a loving one, where the tusker strips the yaa branches to ease his mate's hunger. Aimpathu 32: on his road the tusker pours the little water of a rock pool over his heat-worn mate's head.
teaches: Kuruntokai 37 states the friend's conclusion itself, that the road is loving (அன்பின), while the Aimpathu gives only the tusker's act and leaves the inference to the heroine, so the pair shows the same comfort working first as a stated argument and then as an image she must read.

note: Akananuru 49: the foster mother remembers seeing that the girl who loved her parrot, ball and play-seeds (கிளியும், பந்தும், கழங்கும்) was not as before, without guessing why. Aimpathu 33: the girl no longer thinks of doll, ball, parrot and playmates, and the mother asks whether she will go after her lover.
teaches: In both the neglected playthings are the sign that the girl has passed out of childhood into love, but Akananuru 49 reads the sign too late and dwells on the mother's missed chance, while the venba reads it and turns at once to the burning road, so the pair shows the same evidence serving regret or foreboding.

note: Akananuru 369: after the daughter's elopement her parrot will not drink its milk, her playmates do not play and her doll gets no offering. Aimpathu 33: the girl herself has stopped thinking of doll, ball, parrot and playmates.
teaches: Aimpathu 33 says the girl has forgotten her toys and companions, and Akananuru 369 says those toys and companions still mourn her, so together they show the mother's grief as a forgetting that runs one way: the house keeps faith with a child who has already left it in mind.

note: Kural 1151: if you are not leaving, tell me; if you mean to come back soon, tell it to those who will still be alive. Aimpathu 34: the friend asks the man whether he will cross many wastes of killing robbers, leaving the woman of sword-bright eyes.
teaches: Both are said to the man at the point of departure to stop him, but the Kural argues from the woman's death and the Aimpathu from the man's own danger among robbers, so the pair shows the two levers the dissuading speaker can pull against the journey, her life and his.

note: Akananuru 53: the woman says the man who loves wealth more than her crossed a waste where a red dog rests with its starving mate in the sweet shade of a lettered hero-stone (எழுத்துடை நடுகல் இன்நிழல்). Aimpathu 35: on the road of the man bent on wealth a ghoul gorged on the fat of the slain sleeps in a hero-stone's wide shade.
teaches: In both the hero-stone's shade is the only rest on the wealth-seeker's road, but Akananuru shelters a hungry pair there and the Aimpathu a sated ghoul alone, so the pair shows the stone's shade turned from a picture of shared hardship into one of the road's appetite for men, which is the woman's fear.

note: Akananuru 395: the woman says the man crossed a forest where a fork-horned stag, chasing the mirage, strays off the path and calls for its grazing doe in a failing voice. Aimpathu 36: an elephant pair takes the white mirage for water, runs to it together and falls with tangled legs.
teaches: The two poems take the same chase after a mirage to opposite ends: in Akananuru it parts the stag from its mate and gives the abandoned woman her own cry, in the Aimpathu the pair are fooled and fall together, so the image can either mirror her loneliness or shame the man who leaves when even deceived beasts do not part.

note: Naladiyar 398: the girl answers the friend who asks whether she can walk tomorrow behind her man through the hard forest: one who gets a great horse learns to ride it at once. Aimpathu 37: the mother asks whether the girl who faltered at play can keep pace behind her lover on the stony path. The mother doubts the feet that the girl says love will make able.
teaches: The same question, can her feet go with him, gets opposite answers: the mother measures the girl by her weakness at childhood play, the girl by the man she has gained, so across the two books the pair stages the quarrel of the elopement between the generation that remembers and the one that goes.

note: Akananuru 153: the foster mother says the girl who grew hot and tired even running after a ball with her friends has gone into the burning summer forest, and asks whether her tender feet can manage it (வல்லுநள் கொல்லோ). Aimpathu 37 asks the same with the same verb (வல்லவோ), recalling her faltering at play by the ford.
teaches: The verb வல் and the evidence from play recur in both, which shows the mother's doubt as a set argument of the form: she judges the girl's strength for the road only by her weakness at games, a measure that the girl's going has already overturned.

note: Kalittokai 11: the woman recalls that the man, calling the forest cruel, told her the tusker there lets his mate drink the little muddy water first and the stag gives its own shade to the doe. Aimpathu 38: the stag, judging the pool's little water too scant, feigns drinking so the doe drinks.
teaches: Kalittokai puts the beasts' care in the man's own report, so the woman reasons that one who saw and told it will not let her wither; Aimpathu 38 adds the stag's pretence, a deceit in the service of love, and sets it on the road his heart has already taken, so the same proof is offered from the friend's side and made finer.

note: Akananuru 371: a twist-horned stag whose mate was shot will not drink the little water of the pool (சில்நீர் உண்ணாது) and lies stricken; the man crossing alone sees it and thinks of his love's eyes. Aimpathu 38: the stag feigns drinking the pool's little water so the doe may drink.
teaches: Held together, the two stags at a pool of scant water show the paalai poets making the stag's not drinking the sign of love both while the mate lives and after she dies, and Akananuru 371 bears out the friend's hope in 38, since there the traveller does see such a stag and his thoughts turn home.

note: Akananuru 5: the man tells his heart he gave up the journey when his wife, without a word, showed her grief in her face and her sigh over their son. Aimpathu 39: the man calls his heart foolish, for when they stir to leave for wealth she sobs and sighs; how will she bear it once they are gone?
teaches: Akananuru 5 shows the journey given up on the sight of her mute grief, and Aimpathu 39 shows the man reasoning from her sobs at the setting out to the harder grief to come, so the pair gives the decision against wealth both as what he saw and as what he foresees.

note: Akananuru 167: the man asks his heart whether, after tonight with his wife in the tall mansion, they will lie tomorrow sleepless in the ruined hall of a deserted village. Aimpathu 40: after tonight on the shoulders of her of the cool garland, where will they lie tomorrow, alone beyond the hill paths?
teaches: Akananuru 167 answers its own question with a ruined lodging described in full, while Aimpathu 40 leaves the place unnamed (என்கொலே சேக்கும் இடம்), so the pair shows the same tonight-and-tomorrow argument against the journey working either by the horror of a described shelter or by the bare want of any.

note: Akananuru 50: the hidden-tearful girl says the anril on the palmyra by the house cannot sleep at night if parted even once from its mate. Ainthinai Aimpathu 41: the anril cries though its mate has come and rests beside it.
teaches: The anril's wakefulness is a fixed proof of sleepless separation, and the venba reverses its case: the long poem argues from a parted bird by likeness, the four-line poem from a joined bird by greater reason, so the same bird can carry both the analogy and the a fortiori.

note: In Akananuru 170 the woman begs the crab to carry her word to the shore lord, since grove, backwater and punnai will not speak; in Ainthinai Aimpathu 42 she begs the crab not to trample his chariot's tracks.
teaches: Taken together they show why the crab is the neythal heroine's confidant: it alone moves where the lover moved, so she can ask it either to carry her word to him or to spare the one trace of him she still has.

note: Natrinai 378: the bond began when the shore lord came and broke up their little striped sand-house and spoke soft words. Ainthinai Aimpathu 44: the weeping girl tells her mother that the sea came and wrecked her sand-house.
teaches: Natrinai 378 shows that the wrecked sand-house is the very scene where the secret love began, which turns the girl's excuse in Ainthinai Aimpathu 44 into a coded confession: the 'sea' that broke her play is the man of the sea.

note: Kuruntokai 25: no one but the thief was there, and only a heron watching for aaral fish, so if he lies she has no recourse. Ainthinai Aimpathu 45: will the herons of the grove let his oath go? On a plain reading one heron is no witness and the other herons are.
teaches: The same bird stands at the secret oath in both, but Kuruntokai's heron, intent on its fish, proves that a kalavu vow has no witness, while the venba's herons are made guarantors, so the pair shows the heroine's two answers to the oathless union: despair, or a trust that invents its witnesses.

note: Natrinai 283 and Ainthinai Aimpathu 46 both have the friend ask the shore lord, beside girls decking their sand-houses (with neythal flowers, with pearls), whether it is fitting (தகுமோ, தகுவதோ) that the girl's beauty should waste.
teaches: The friend's reproach has a fixed form, the girls' sand-house play set against the heroine's wasting beauty with the question 'is it fitting?', and Natrinai adds the ground the venba leaves implicit: his word was held truer than the sun, so the wasting is a breach of his truth.

note: In Akananuru 80 the friend tells the shore lord that they spend the day scaring birds from the fish their father brought, and bids him come by day; in Ainthinai Aimpathu 47 the hero sees the girl scaring birds from the fish her brothers brought and finds her a tormenting goddess.
teaches: Guarding the drying catch is the neythal girl's appointed work and so the one place she is seen by day: the friend can offer it as a meeting place, while the hero's first sight of her there already places her among the kinsmen whose catch she guards, which is why the sight brings fear.

note: Naladiyar 203: the great never say they will not support those who have come to depend on them (தற்சேர்ந் தவரை), as a branch bears its own fruit. Ainthinai Aimpathu 48: can those who do not hold to the distress of those who have come to depend on them (தற்சேர்ந்தார்) carry great renown?
teaches: The shared word தற்சேர்ந்தார் shows the friend borrowing the maxim of supporting one's dependents and turning it on the lover: the girl in secret love is made a dependent with a kinsman's claim, and his renown is staked on marrying her.

note: In Akananuru 4 the returning man has tied his chariot's bell-tongues so as not to startle the paired birds sleeping in the flowering boughs; in Ainthinai Aimpathu 50 the waiting girl takes the noise of birds for his horses' bells.
teaches: Held together, the two poems make the chariot bell the sound by which each lover's attention is measured: the man who has come home to his wife silences it out of care for mated birds, while the girl still in secret love hears it in every bird.

note: Natrinai 57: while the herd of wild cows sleeps with their calves, a female monkey creeps up, squeezes the swollen udder and wrings the milk into her young one's hands. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 3: the monkey strokes the udder and the wild cow, glad as with her calf, lets the milk flow.
teaches: Held together they show one scene turned from theft to gift: the older poem's monkey steals while the cows sleep, fitting a friend who warns of the girl's ruin, while the later venba makes the cow consent, fitting a girl who says she cannot part, so the speaker's case decides whether the milk is stolen or given.

note: Kural 782: the friendship (கேண்மை) of the wise waxes like the crescent moon, that of fools wanes. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 4: the friendship of the worthy (சான்றவர் கேண்மை) stands firm and grows into strength, so the mountain lord's will too.
teaches: The venba lifts the Kural's maxim about friendship with the worthy into a girl's mouth as her proof that her lover will not fail, which shows the ethics books' rule of friendship being used, within the akam frame, to judge a lover's character before marriage.

note: Kural 1102: the man says the jewelled woman (அணியிழை) is herself the medicine for the sickness she causes. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 5: the friend tells the man there is no medicine but him for the bright-jewelled girl (வயங்கிழை).
teaches: The same paradox of the lover as the only cure runs in both directions, the woman for the man in the Kural, the man for the woman here, and the change of speaker turns the Kural's private wonder into the friend's demand that he give the cure.

note: Akananuru 318: the friend tells the man who comes alone at night by a path made fearful by elephants, snakes and tigers not to come from today, and to blow his horn on reaching home so they know he is safe. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 10: the girl asks her friend to tell the lord of the snake-haunted groves not to come by night, to keep a life safe.
teaches: The long poem spells out what the four lines only hint, that refusing the night meeting is an act of care for the man's life on a dangerous path, and the venba moves the plea into the girl's own wish (குறையொன்று உடையேன்), showing the same refusal felt from inside.

note: Akananuru 242: the mother, not knowing of the man who chased parrots from the millet with them, calls the ignorant velan, and before the kid's life is given he should come and embrace the girl. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 12: parrots raid the millet, the girl has embraced him fully, and the velan has resolved to cut the kid.
teaches: Both set the embrace against the kid's sacrifice, but the older poem makes the embrace the remedy that must come before the rite, while the venba gives both as done, which leaves the velan preparing a useless sacrifice for a cure already taken.

note: Kural 1233: the shoulders that swelled on the day of union now announce loudly that he has gone. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 14: because he is said to be good, her shoulders have forgotten to waste even if he leaves.
teaches: On a plain reading the two make incompatible claims about the same sign: the Kural takes wasting shoulders as the body's certain witness to separation, while the venba says trust in the man's goodness can stop the body from giving that witness at all.

note: Both close on 'each time I see the sky' and the eye: Aimpathu 5 says drops mingle and fall from the eye (துளிகலந்து வீழ்தருங் கண்); Ezhupathu 15 says the eye tosses with water as the sky tosses with clouds (நீரோ(டு) அலமரும் கண்).
teaches: The shared closing formula could match eye and sky in two different ways, by substance in Aimpathu (tears are the rain's drops) and by motion in Ezhupathu (the eye tosses as the sky tosses), so the formula fixed the pairing but left the basis of the likeness to the poet.

note: Kural 1224: with the lover absent, evening comes like enemies to a killing ground. Ezhupathu 17: as kodal buds and thunder greet the rains, the little evening comes like killers so that those with no one to embrace them tremble.
teaches: The Kural's image of evening as executioner, spoken by one woman of one absent man, appears in the Ezhupathu tied to the rainy season and widened to a class (those with no one to hold them), which shows the image was a mullai convention of the promised-return season before or beside its use as a private complaint.

note: Aimpathu 6: the bee humming at the jasmine is sweet to those who have someone to lean on, but the dark evening comes and saws at us who have no one. Ezhupathu 17: the evening comes like killers upon those with no one to embrace them.
teaches: Aimpathu 6 states both halves of the rule, sweet to the partnered and cutting to the lone, while Ezhupathu 17 states only the second, so together they show that the evening's cruelty was located in the hearer's state, not in the hour, and the later poem could leave the happy half unsaid.

note: Kural 1226: she did not know, while her husband had not yet gone, that evening brings sickness. Ezhupathu 21: before he returns, the evening comes with the rains to torment her, and no one lives in such folly as she.
teaches: The Kural names the woman's ignorance at the time of parting as the cause of her suffering, while the Ezhupathu's மடம் is a folly she still lives in now, knowing the evening, so the pairing separates ignorance that excuses from folly that the speaker mocks in herself.

note: Kural 1228: the herdsman's flute is an envoy of the burning evening and a weapon that kills. Ezhupathu 22: herdsmen blow konrai flutes, the herd goes in, evening comes as she watches, and the sky thunders and draws its bow.
teaches: The Kural makes the herdsman's flute the evening's envoy and weapon, and Ezhupathu 22, which names no pain at all, gives the same evening a second weapon, the rainbow drawn as a bow, so the reader of the Kural sees that the evening's arming was a scene the venba poets could show without comment.

note: Aimpathu 7: after the cattle have fed, the herdsman's glad flute at the red evening is like a spear thrown at her. Ezhupathu 22: the herdsmen's konrai flutes and the herd entering the fold are only watched, with no feeling stated.
teaches: Aimpathu 7 states the wound the herdsman's dusk flute gives, and Ezhupathu 22 relies on it unstated, so read together they show that by these short anthologies the homecoming herd and flute were enough on their own to signal the waiting wife's pain.

note: Both mothers lament a daughter gone with a man through the bowmen's wasteland; Akananuru 35 prays to the god that the stranger may adorn her and lull her on his chest, while Ainthinai Ezhupathu 30 can only wonder whether the girl pines or walks on behind him with reddened feet.
teaches: Together they give the mother's lament two stages, first not knowing whether the girl regrets her going and then accepting it and praying for the man's care, so the venba catches the moment the Akananuru poem has already passed.

note: In Akananuru 91 the elephant that shrinks with its hungry mate in drought lets the friend reassure the heroine after the man has gone; in Ainthinai Ezhupathu 31 the elephant sleeping with its mate in the burning forest comes when the man only speaks of going, and her tears answer it.
teaches: The same iraicchi of the elephant pair keeping together in the heat serves to comfort after the parting and to dissuade before it, which shows the image carries the lovers' bond itself and the speaker turns it to whatever the moment needs.

note: Akananuru 53: past the lettered hero-stone of men felled by the archers' fine arrows, the heroine says his love is for wealth more than for her (பொருளே காதலர் காதல்). Ainthinai Ezhupathu 32 keeps the lettered stones, the archers' fine arrows and the claim that his love's longing has become hard-won wealth.
teaches: The venba compresses Akananuru 53's scene and accusation into four lines but drops the friend's defence that he goes from a giving heart, putting his 'fitting labour' in its place, so the later poem shows which part of the older argument had become formula and which part it chose to change.

note: Akananuru 35's road is held by bowmen of வில் ஏர் வாழ்க்கை, 'the life whose plough is the bow', and their cairns; Ainthinai Ezhupathu 33's road by வில்லுழுது உண்பார், 'those who eat by ploughing with the bow', among the cairns.
teaches: Held together they show the bow-as-plough figure for the wasteland robbers passing intact from the Sangam anthology into the later venba, while its use shifts from a mother's fear for a daughter on the road to a wife's reproach that the man can see the road's dangers but not her.

note: In Kural 1247 the woman in separation tells her heart to give up either desire or shame, since she cannot bear both; in Ainthinai Ezhupathu 34 she foresees her heart throwing off shame and going with her life after him.
teaches: The couplet poses the choice between desire and shame as a demand on the heart, and the venba shows the heart's answer and its cost, since choosing desire there means the life leaving the body with it.

note: In Akananuru 297 the man on his way for wealth sees a wildcat's fluffy kitten following its mother like stars round the moon; in Ainthinai Ezhupathu 40 the heroine hears that on his road the spotted wildcat watches for prey for its kitten.
teaches: Each lover sees the wildcat with its young on the wealth road from his or her own side, the man as the household he leaves behind and the woman as the provision he goes to win, so the creature gathers both halves of the paalai argument about leaving for wealth.

note: Kural 1203: a sneeze that seems to come and then dies away makes her think he seems about to think of her and does not. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 41: sneezes come one after another, so he is thinking of her. On the plain reading the same sign gives opposite verdicts.
teaches: Both women read the sneeze by the same folk belief, but the Kural uses its failure for a wry doubt while the venba piles it up as proof, which shows the belief was firm enough to support either despair or hope depending on what the body did.

note: In Akananuru 289 the man on his journey imagines her praying 'speak good' each time the lizard chirps; in Ainthinai Ezhupathu 42 the lizard chirps at the favourable side, together with a throbbing eye and good dreams.
teaches: The man's imagined picture of her waiting on the lizard and her own report that the lizard has spoken well are the two ends of one practice, which shows that the omen was a shared language the separated lovers each expected the other to be reading.
audit_text_issue: Line 3 'மெள்தோள்' and 'பிணைதீர' are uncertain.

note: In Kalittokai 85 the mother shares out her milk in mockery to the 'other mothers' who wept after trusting the father's deceiving oath (மாயச் சூள்); in Ainthinai Ezhupathu 44 a woman says she believed his words long ago, not knowing them for a false oath (பொய்ச்சூள்).
teaches: Read together, the false oath is the wound the wife shares with her rivals: Kalittokai's mother pities the other women it deceived, and the venba's speaker finds herself among them, so the oath binds all the man's women in one injury.

note: Kalittokai 79: the wife tells the husband not to take up their son, whose hands will pull the pearl chain and garland by which the other women marked him (அணி சிதைப்பான்). Ainthinai Ezhupathu 45: he comes with the son on his chest, the boy's pearl ornaments crushing his frontlet (பட்டஞ் சிதைப்ப).
teaches: Kalittokai spells out what the four-line poem only shows: the son's hands spoiling the father's finery are spoiling the other women's tokens, so the venba's ironic 'he is resourceful' means the child he brings as a shield is also the one who exposes him.
