note: Natrinai 380: refusing the bard, the friend says they smell of ghee, smoke and new birth, holding the son with milk at the breast, and are no match for the man of the bright-jewelled women's street. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 47: the wife says the son is suckled and she is old, and sends the bard to the street of the budding-breasted women.
teaches: The pair shows that the nursing mother's body is a set argument in refusing the go-between: the friend in Natrinai offers it as humble unfitness, the wife in the venba turns it into scorn by sending the bard to dance for his food, so the same motherhood can be pleaded as modesty or thrown as contempt.

note: Akananuru 46: the friend refusing the husband entry describes his town's red-eyed buffalo breaking its tether in the night, scattering fish and grazing the lotus. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 49: the red-eyed buffalo breaks its wooden clog, eats the field crop and rests in the shade, and the bard is told to carry this to the flower-like women.
teaches: The same hidden comparison is aimed at different hearers: in Akananuru 46 it shames the husband at the door, in the venba it is sent through the bard to the other women as a warning, which shows the buffalo ullurai was a portable accusation that could be addressed to either party of the triangle.

note: Natrinai 330: the male buffalo plunges into the pond and rests from the day's labour in the sweet shade of the marutham (இன் நிழல் வதியும்), and the friend blames the courtesans' mean hearts. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 49: the buffalo breaks its clog, eats the crop and then rests in the shade (நிழல்வதியும்).
teaches: The resting buffalo is innocent after labour in Natrinai and guilty after plunder in the venba, and the blame follows suit, falling on the courtesans in one and on the husband in the other, so what the beast did before the shade decides whom the poem accuses.

note: Akananuru 66: the husband, dressed to wed another, is drawn home by the little son who runs to his chariot, and the wife says the old saying about sons has proved true. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 51: the wife sends the bard away, saying her little son with gold bangles is her companion.
teaches: The son works on both sides of the marutham quarrel: in Akananuru 66 he pulls the straying father back into the house, in the venba the wife holds him up as companion enough to refuse the father's go-between, so the child is at once the husband's way in and the wife's reason to keep him out.

note: Kural 773 calls generous help to a fallen foe (ஊராண்மை) the cutting edge of valour. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 52: the friend mocks the husband for treating his going to the other street as ஊராண்மை, manliness before the town.
teaches: The Kural makes ஊராண்மை a virtue of restraint toward the weak, while the friend uses the same word for the husband's public swagger in neglecting his wife, so on a plain reading the two give the word opposite contents, and the venba's sarcasm depends on the higher sense the Kural fixes.

note: Kural 572: the world's ways rest on கண்ணோட்டம், and those without it are a burden on the earth. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 54: the husband who resolves to withhold கண்ணோட்டம் while taking the wife's devoted service is told the blame falls on him.
teaches: The Kural states kindly regard as a duty of public life; the venba brings it inside the marriage and makes its withdrawal a husband's blame, which shows the ethical term was already at work in the language of domestic quarrel.

note: Akananuru 146: refusing the bard, the wife asks who the woman will be who now trusts the deceiving philanderer and will weep and pale as she did. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 55: the wife tells the other women directly not to embrace him to love's end or pine for him, but to give up their longing.
teaches: Akananuru 146 only pities the next woman from a distance, while the venba turns to the rivals and counsels them, so together they show the wife's grievance passing into a warning to the women who will suffer as she did.
audit_text_issue: Akananuru 146 line 8 அனியள் looks like a misprint for அளியள், and line 6 ஒள்ளிமழை for ஒள்ளிழை.

note: Ainkurunuru 65: the wife tells the husband not to embrace her body that bore their son, since it would spoil his chest. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 56: with the son trampling him, he praises her slackened breast, though he presses the budding breasts of a girl elsewhere.
teaches: In both the body that bore the son is the ground of the wife's sulking: in Ainkurunuru she withholds it as unfit for his groomed chest, in the venba she sees his praise of it as a cover for his taste for younger bodies, so the mother's body is what she bars him from and what he flatters to come back.
audit_text_issue: Lines 3-4 (என்னுடைய பாவை வளர்முலைக் கண்ஞமுக்குவார்) are obscure; speaker and referent uncertain.

note: Kalittokai 85 says the father uses the lying bard as a fishhook to bind the hearts of the women he wants. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 50 tells the bard to go on without pause to the street of the gold-like women.
teaches: Kalittokai names the bard as the husband's lure for other women, which explains the venba's order to keep going to that street: the wife is sending the go-between back to his real work, so refusing the bard and accusing him are one act.

note: Ainthinai Aimpathu 50: the heroine says she rose at what she took for his horses' bells and turned back on hearing it was birds. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 59 tells the same mistake of her in the third person, with the same words புள்ளரவம் கேட்டுப் பெயர்ந்.
teaches: The two venbas share a stock scene, and the second adds what the first leaves out: in the heroine's own telling she turns back from a melting heart, in the onlooker's telling from fear of the hamlet's talk, so the formula carried either the private grief or the public danger of kalavu waiting.

note: Natrinai 335: the sea's sound never stops and the tide comes and goes, and with the anril and the lute the night cannot be survived. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 60: the sea, like her, does not sleep as the tide shifts, because the shore lord took her beauty and left.
teaches: In the Natrinai the restless sea is one of the things that keep the heroine awake, while the venba makes the same tide sleepless for her own reason, so the pair shows the neythal sea turning from a cause of sleeplessness into a fellow sufferer.

note: Kuruntokai 25: no one was there but the thief, only a heron watching for aaral fish on the day he took her. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 62: does the heron of the grove not know his cruelty, though it saw him go and turn graceless?
teaches: Kuruntokai's heron proves that the secret union had no witness worth the name, and the venba goes one step on, upbraiding that same silent witness for not knowing what it saw, so the heron of kalavu moves from absent proof to complicit bystander.

note: Ainthinai Aimpathu 45: will the herons of the grove let his oath go unpunished? Ainthinai Ezhupathu 62: the heron of the grove saw his cruelty and does not know it. On a plain reading one makes the herons guarantors of his oath and the other finds the heron a useless witness.
teaches: Held together, the two shore venbas show the heroine's trust in the grove's herons as witnesses of a secret oath collapsing once he has gone: the birds she counted on to hold him are the birds she then reproaches for seeing nothing.

note: Kuruntokai 236: the friend tells the shore lord to go if he must, but first give back the beauty he consumed (நீ உண்டவென் னலனே). Ainthinai Ezhupathu 63: the heroine would accost him herself and say 'give back the colour' (வண்ணந்தா).
teaches: The demand to give back consumed beauty belongs to the friend in Kuruntokai, but the venba puts it in the heroine's own mouth and doubts that only looking at him would suffice, so the pair shows the reproach moving from the go-between to the injured woman herself.

note: Both poems end on the same demand, வண்ணம் தா ... தொடுத்து: in 63 the heroine and her friend would accost the shore lord themselves; in 65 she sends the paired anril to say it.
teaches: Two poems of one sequence ending on the same words show the demand for her colour passing from a plan to face him to a message given to a bird, which tells us how far her confidence in meeting him has fallen.

note: Ainthinai Aimpathu 42: the heroine begs the crab not to blur the tracks of his chariot so she can gaze at the path he took. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 64: she tells the stork that it knows the path by which he went.
teaches: In both venbas the path of the departed shore lord is known only to the shore's creatures, the crab who can erase it and the stork who has seen it, so the pair shows the neythal heroine's knowledge of his leaving lodged entirely in what the animals of the beach can keep or destroy.

note: Akananuru 170: since grove, backwater and punnai will not speak, the woman begs the crab to carry her word to the shore lord, at midnight when the sea-crow dreams beside its mate. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 65: she bids the anril, joined with its mate, to tell him 'give back the colour'.
teaches: The long poem shows why a creature is her messenger, since the land itself is mute, while the venba chooses a messenger whose own paired life is the reproach, so together they show the creature-messenger used first for its reach and then for its example.
audit_text_issue: Ainthinai Ezhupathu 65 is marked uncertain.

note: Kural 1157: do not the bangles slipping from my wrist spread the news that the shore lord has left me? Ainthinai Ezhupathu 66: will the thief-hearted shore lord walk off by another path while her good bangles slip?
teaches: The couplet makes the slipping bangle a herald announcing his departure, while the venba places it at the moment of his going and calls his heart a thief's, so the pair qualifies the Kural's sign: the bangle that tells the town of his leaving also convicts him of planned deceit.

note: Akananuru 380: the shore lord, wooing, showed the girls a crab carrying a naaval fruit to its mate in its burrow and said 'this is a fine way'. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 68: the friend tells the shore lord of the crab with its mate on the dune, and that her friend has paled.
teaches: In the Akananuru the hero himself offers the crab that cares for its mate as a sign of how he will behave, and in the venba the friend returns the same crab to him as a reproach while the girl pales, so the pair shows a courting pledge turned into the evidence against the man who gave it.

note: Kural 1182 has pallor ride the woman's body proud that 'he gave it'; Kainnilai 1 has her body waste pale as if saying 'the forest lord joined with her'.
teaches: Set in the guarded millet field of the secret love, the Kural's private conceit of pallor naming its giver becomes a public danger, since a body that names the lover undoes the secrecy that kalavu depends on.

note: Both set a hill creature that has handled ripe fruit against snares; in Kuruntokai the hunter sets nets on every tree after the fruit is already touched, in Kainnilai the monkey tastes the fruit and is caught.
teaches: The same fruit-and-snare economy of the hill serves two speakers opposite ways: the friend uses the late snares to tell the man the girl is now guarded too late, while the girl uses the caught monkey to say she herself is the one bound by the sweetness she tasted.

note: Kuruntokai 42's friend asks the hero whether their bond will wane even if desire ends; Kainnilai 4's friend asks the girl whether he is one to join and then forget.
teaches: The one doubt about the man's constancy is put by the friend as a challenge to him in Kuruntokai and as a comfort to the girl in Kainnilai, so the pair shows the friend's double office of pressing the hero and calming the heroine with the same question.

note: Kural 1249's woman asks her heart whom it goes seeking when he is within it; Kainnilai 6's girl lets her heart go unspoken to his jewelled chest.
teaches: The heart's going out to the lover is chided as foolish in the Kural's separation chapter but is a silent secret gift in Kainnilai's secret stage, so the same movement of the heart is judged by whether he is still near.

note: In Kural 1157 the slipping bangles proclaim that the lord of the shore has left; in Kainnilai 7 they slip at the mere telling of the hill lord's friendship.
teaches: The Kural gives the bangles as a sign without a scene, and Kainnilai supplies the scene that explains them: a monkey that snatches the fruit and bolts, so the bangles fall because the 'friendship' was a theft and the leaving was already in it.

note: Both have the hill lord of the vengai coming at midnight with spear in hand; Kainnilai 10 is the girl's eager forecast, Akananuru 298 her words when he has come, sweet yet unable to speak her love for fear of the mother.
teaches: Read together the two give the before and after of the night tryst: the quatrain's sleepless certainty that he will come turns, once he is there, into fear of the household and a plea for marriage, so the midnight visit is never the end the girl longs for.

note: Kural 1151: the friend (or the woman) tells the man that his promise of a quick return should be told to those still alive then. Kainnilai 13: told of his going by the long wasteland, her eyes went soft with tears.
teaches: Both answer the man's announcement of departure, but the Kural puts the threat to her life into argued words while the Kainnilai lets the friend report only the eyes giving way on hearing, so the pair shows the same reply could be made as a sharp argument or as a bare bodily fact laid before him.
audit_text_issue: Line 1 'கடுகி அதர்அலைக்கும்' is hard to construe.

note: Akananuru 387: on the road, a lizard's small click by the hero-stones makes even lords with elephants halt and turn back. Kainnilai 18: at home, the truthful lizard chirps as if it has seen the traveller's return.
teaches: Held together they show that the lizard's voice was trusted at both ends of the journey with opposite force, as a warning that turns travellers back on the road and as a promise of return to those at home, so the omen's sense depended on which way the hearer faced.

note: Akananuru 351: the returning man imagines the lizard that chirps whenever she thinks of him sounding at her ear as medicine for her aching shoulders. Kainnilai 18: the friend tells her the truthful lizard has chirped, seeing the traveller come.
teaches: The man in the Akananuru counts on the lizard to announce him and the friend in the Kainnilai reports that it has, so the pair gives both halves of one belief, that the traveller's approach reaches home through the lizard before he does.

note: Kural 1265: the pallor of her shoulders will leave only after she has seen her husband with her eyes. Kainnilai 19: the friend says the brightness returning to her forehead shows he is coming, before he has come.
teaches: On the Kural's reading the body recovers only from the sight of him and news cannot cure it, while the Kainnilai friend reads a recovery already begun as a sign of his return, so the two disagree on whether the body answers his presence or foreknows it.

note: Kural 1249: the woman asks her heart whom it goes out looking for, since the beloved is already within it. Kainnilai 21: the woman says her heart has gone after the man, swimming the long way through the scorched forest.
teaches: Both women speak of a heart that leaves to follow the man, but the Kural calls that going needless because he lives inside her, while the Kainnilai takes the heart's long swim as real, so the pair sets an inward answer to absence against the older picture of the heart travelling the road.

note: Kainnilai 21: the woman says her heart swims the long way after him (நீந்து). Kainnilai 22: the friend says he will swim back over the old clefts (நீந்திப் பெயர்ந்தவர்) and they will soon see him.
teaches: Read in sequence, the friend answers the woman's image with her own verb turned round, the heart swimming outward becoming the man swimming home, which shows how the friend's comfort in this book works by reversing the heroine's words rather than contradicting them.

note: Akananuru 29: the returned man tells his wife that only his body stayed in the burning waste for the work, while his foolish heart was with her. Kainnilai 22: the friend asks whether she thinks the heart of the man who crossed the robber forest has parted from her.
teaches: The friend's question in the Kainnilai presumes exactly what the man asserts on his return in the Akananuru, that the body went and the heart stayed, so the pair shows the body-heart split was a shared assurance used by the comforter before and by the man after the journey.

note: Natrinai 84: the woman reports that he will go (they say) by the hard waste where the mirage lures the deer, and excuses him as one who cannot live a home life unable to relieve beggars. Kainnilai 24: the woman reports that the hard waste where the deer runs after the mirage is, they say, the road of the loveless one.
teaches: The same reported road with the same mirage-chasing deer ends in opposite verdicts on the man, a duty that excuses him in the Natrinai and a want of love that condemns him in the Kainnilai, so the landscape fixed the scene while the poet chose the moral.

note: Kar Narpathu 21: the returning man says the mullai buds along the road stand sharp like the teeth of his simple girl (முள்ளெயிறு ஏய்ப்ப). Kainnilai 25: the friend shows the heroine the mullai putting out sharp teeth (கூர்எயிறு ஈன) as proof he will come.
teaches: One bud is read at both ends of the waiting: on the road the man sees her teeth in it, at home the friend offers it to her as his promise kept, so the mullai's teeth tie the two absent lovers to a single sight.
audit_text_issue: Kar Narpathu 21's colophon reads தலைமகள் பாகற்குச் சொல்லியது, likely an error for தலைமகன், since the speaker rides the chariot.

note: Kar Narpathu 26: the thondri blooms over every field like the first-night lamps of Karthigai, and the rain comes as messenger. Kainnilai 26: the blood-red thonri buds are so like fire that a bird shies from them.
teaches: Both friends read the red thonri as flame, but one sees festival lamps and the other a fire that frightens, so the same sign of return can carry welcome or alarm, and the Kainnilai friend lets a trace of fear into her comfort.
audit_text_issue: Kainnilai 26 line 2 is partly lost.

note: Kural 1182: the woman says pallor rides over her body (மேனிமேல் ஊரும் பசப்பு), claiming it is his gift. Kainnilai 27: at the rainy evening, thinking of his coming, pallor spreads over her body (ஊர்தரு மேனி பசப்பு).
teaches: The couplet says only that pallor rides her body by his right; the Kainnilai fragment gives it an hour and a cause, the rain-season evening and the thought of his coming, so expectation, not only absence, is what sets the pallor moving.
audit_text_issue: kainnilai:27 lines 1-2 are lost; only ஒல்கப் புகுதரு survives.

note: Akananuru 23: in the rains the stag embraces his doe (பிணை ... தழீஇ), and the woman asks if this is the time her man meant. Kainnilai 29: kurunthu blooms, the stag embraces his doe and the rain-cloud thunders; the rest is lost.
teaches: The Akananuru poem shows the stag's embrace being weighed as the promised season's clock, which tells a reader of the broken Kainnilai verse what such an embrace was there to measure, even though its own ending is gone.
audit_text_issue: Kainnilai 29 lines 1, 3 and 4 are lost or partly lost.

note: Akananuru 14: the wife asks what will become of them by morning if he does not remember even in the evening when the cattle crowd into the common (மன்றுநிறை புகுதரும் மாலையும்). Kainnilai 30: the hour when the cowherds with konrai pipes enter the common (மன்றம் புகுதரும் போழ்து).
teaches: The Akananuru wife names the homecoming to the common as the hour by which a man who remembers would be back, which explains why the Kainnilai poet could mark the waiting by that hour alone: the village's return is the measure of his not returning.
audit_text_issue: Kainnilai 30 lines 1-2 are lost (lacuna).

note: Kar Narpathu 22: the returning man says the plumed, spirited horses are yoked (உளையணிந்து ... கலிமாவும் பூட்டிய). Kainnilai 33: the friend says he will come yoking his fine spirited plumed horses (உளையார் கலிநன் மாப்பூட்டி வருவார்).
teaches: The friend's promise uses nearly the words with which the hero himself reports setting out, so the comfort at home is shown to be an accurate picture of what is happening on the road, and the formula passes between the friend's and the hero's mouths.
audit_text_issue: Kainnilai 33 lines 1-2 are lost (lacuna).

note: Kar Narpathu 33: the man says he set as his sign the time when the cloud that drew up the sea (கடனீர் முகந்த) would gather on the western hill. Kainnilai 34: as the cloud that scooped the sea pours (கடல்முகந்து கார்பொழிய), the lover has come.
teaches: Held together, the two verses close the loop of the mullai promise: one poet's hero names the sea-drinking cloud as his appointed sign, and the other poet has the lover arrive exactly as that cloud breaks.
audit_text_issue: kainnilai:34 lines 1, 2 and 4 are largely lost.

note: Akananuru 74: the heroine says she could bear the friend's comfort but for the harsh small pipe the unlettered cowherds blow (கல்லாக் கோவலர் ஊதும் வல்வாய் சிறுகுழல்) at evening. Kainnilai 35: the herders who do not know (தெரிவிலர்) blow the sweet pipe (தீங்குழல்).
teaches: Both poets excuse the herders by their ignorance, but one calls the pipe harsh and the other sweet, which shows that the cruelty is not in the sound itself but in the hour and the ear that hears it.
audit_text_issue: Kainnilai 35 lines 1-2 lost and line 4 broken (அரித)

note: Kural 1228: the herdsman's flute is the messenger of the burning evening and a weapon that kills (கொல்லும் படை). Kainnilai 35: the herders, heedless, blow the sweet pipe at that hour.
teaches: The couplet makes the flute a weapon; the Kainnilai adds that those who wield it do not know they are wounding anyone, so the evening's weapon kills without a killer who intends it.
audit_text_issue: Kainnilai 35 lines 1-2 are lost and line 4 breaks off at அரித. | Lines 1-2 are lacunose and line 4 breaks off (அரித); the sense is a reconstruction.

note: Ainthinai Ezhupathu 49: the wife tells the bard to carry to the other women the man's description as lord of the town where the red-eyed buffalo breaks its clog, sinks into the pond and gorges on the crop. Kainnilai 37: the rutting buffalo plunges into the pond before the wife tells the bard to stop lying.
teaches: Ainthinai Ezhupathu 49 tells the bard to deliver the buffalo as the man's own portrait, which shows that in Kainnilai 37 the same plunging buffalo set before the bard is a character sketch of the husband and not just the setting of his town.

note: Ainkurunuru 43: the woman tells the man his bard is a bigger liar than he is and swears many oaths. Kainnilai 37: the wife tells the bard to stop pouring out lies before her.
teaches: Ainkurunuru 43 ranks the bard's lying above the man's, and Kainnilai 37 lets her silence the bard directly while the man is only named, so together they show the wife's anger moving onto the go-between as the safer target.

note: Kural 1311: the woman refuses the chest of the man she calls a philanderer, because all women feed on him with their eyes. Kainnilai 38: the wife bars him from her house from today because he lives desiring young women's shoulders.
teaches: The couplet's refusal rests on a witty pretext, that other women merely look at him, while the venba's rests on his actual desire for other women, so the pair shows the Kural turning a real grievance of the marutham poems into the fine point of a lovers' quarrel.
audit_text_issue: Kainnilai 38 line 4 lacuna; line 3 துயிலின் obscure

note: Natrinai 250: the man tells the bard how, coming near to hug his toddling son, his wife took it otherwise and shied away. Kainnilai 39: the wife says he comes bringing the garlanded son, pointing to him, to torment her. On the man's telling the son is a real tenderness she misreads; on hers it is a tactic.
teaches: Read together the two poems give both sides of the same approach through the child, the husband insisting his affection was misjudged and the wife calling it harassment, so neither poem's account can be taken as the plain fact of the scene.

note: Ainthinai Ezhupathu 50: the wife calls it folly that he seeks entry with the son as his backing. Kainnilai 39: he comes with the garlanded son, pointing to him, to trouble her.
teaches: Ainthinai Ezhupathu 50 names the son as the man's 'witness' (துணைச்சான்றோன்) and Kainnilai 39 shows the boy dressed in a garland and pointed out, so the pair shows the child being staged as evidence of the marriage the husband has broken.

note: Ainthinai Ezhupathu 51: speaking of the man of the good pond town is my grief; get up and go, bard; I have my little son as companion. Kainnilai 41 opens with the same line (பொய்கைநல் லூரன் திறன்கிளப்ப) and ends with the little son as what she owns.
teaches: The two venbas share their first line and their closing son, but where Ainthinai Ezhupathu 51 calls the man's praise her grief (எவ்வம்), Kainnilai 41 says she already knows his doings, so the reworking turns the wife's pain into a cool dismissal while keeping the son as her answer.

note: Kalittokai 81: the wife asks the toddling son to repeat the words the 'mothers' of the big street taught him, and the husband blames the bard. Kainnilai 41: she knows his doings, having the sweet babbling son as her own.
teaches: Kalittokai 81 shows a son's prattle betraying where his father has taken him, which supports reading Kainnilai 41's 'we know' as knowledge gained from the boy's babble rather than only as a mother's comfort.

note: Ainthinai Ezhupathu 47: the wife tells the greasy-mouthed bard to go to the street of young women and eat there even if he must dance for it (கூத்தாடி உண்ணினும் உண்). Kainnilai 42: if he is in want, let the bard take the man as his dancer, make him dance and eat even so (ஆட்டுவித்து உண்ணினும் உண்).
teaches: The closing formula is the same, but Kainnilai moves the dancing from the bard to the husband, so the pair shows the later poet sharpening the taunt into a picture of the man as a performer worked by others.

note: Kainnilai 42: the bard may make the man his dancer. Kainnilai 46: the man spoke pleasantly and only seemed ashamed.
teaches: Verse 46 says his shame was a show and verse 42 makes him a dancer, so the decade presents the husband's contrition as performance from both sides, his own acting and the bard's staging.

note: Ainthinai Ezhupathu 47: the son has been fed and we are old now (மூத்தேம் இனியாம்); go to the young women's street. Kainnilai 45: we are old now, bard (மூத்தேம் இனிப்பாண), young before, and we did not know he would leave.
teaches: Ainthinai Ezhupathu 47 offers age as the reason he goes to younger women, while Kainnilai 45 sets the same words against his old promises, so the pair shows the formula of the ageing wife used once to explain his straying and once to expose a betrayal she could not foresee.

note: Kainnilai 45: we are old now and did not know he would leave. Kainnilai 48: grown old with sagging breasts, we want no answer from him.
teaches: In 45 her age is the vantage from which she sees his promises were false, and in 48 it becomes the ground of her refusal, so the decade moves age from grief to a reason for closing the door.
audit_text_issue: kainnilai:48 line 2 பொலிவுடைத்தா is unclear.

note: Thinaimalai 131: the wife tells the graceless bard he need not fashion words to begin a reconciliation; she turned the day she heard the man's lies. Kainnilai 46: the man spoke many pleasant things and seemed ashamed; useless bard, say nothing false and go.
teaches: Thinaimalai 131 dates her refusal to the lies she heard, while Kainnilai 46 adds that the man had already acted out his shame, so the pair shows the bard's plea coming after the husband's own performance has failed.

note: Kuruntokai 127: because the man's one bard proved a liar, every bard looks like a thief to the women he left. Kainnilai 47: the wife calls the bard a liar (பொய்ப் பாண) and bars him from her house.
teaches: Kuruntokai 127 states the general effect of one lying go-between and Kainnilai 47 shows its consequence in a single house, the door shut to the bard himself, so the pair shows distrust of the messenger hardening into exclusion.
audit_text_issue: kainnilai:47 lines 1-2 hard to construe.

note: Natrinai 380: the friend refuses the bard, saying our breasts ooze milk, we smell of new birth and are no match for the man of the jewelled women's street. Kainnilai 48: the man does not embrace the sandal-cool breasts; we have grown old with sagging breasts; come for no answer.
teaches: Natrinai 380 makes motherhood the wife's disqualification and Kainnilai 48 makes age, so the pair shows the wife's body at two stages of marriage offered in the same mocking way as the reason the man has gone elsewhere.

note: Kuruntokai 25: no one was there but the thief and a heron watching for aaral fish on the day he took her, so what can she do if he lies. Kainnilai 50: she will tell neither him nor the anril, only the stork of the grove that saw his hard oath.
teaches: The heron that in Kuruntokai only proves how alone the heroine was becomes, in the venba, the one hearer she trusts with the broken oath, so the bird witness of kalavu moves from a sign of her helplessness to the only court left to her.

note: Ainthinai Ezhupathu 62: does the heron of the grove not know his cruelty, though it saw him turn graceless? Kainnilai 50: the stork of the grove, which saw his harsh oath, is the one she bids listen.
teaches: The two shore venbas value the same bird witness in opposite ways, reproached for seeing and not knowing once the oath is broken, confided in because it saw while she still hopes the oath can be held, so the witness's worth follows the stage of her trust.

note: Natrinai 167: the friend refuses the bard who came with the shore lord's message (துறைவன் தூதொடும் வந்த ... பணி மொழி). Kainnilai 51 uses the same words for a bird (தூதொடு வந்த பணிமொழிப் புள்ளே) and tells it to fly off.
teaches: The formula that names the bard refused at the door is given in the venba to a bird, showing the short form compressing the social scene of வாயில் மறுத்தல் into a creature of the shore while keeping the old wording.
audit_text_issue: Kainnilai 51 line 2 is partly lost (dots in the source).

note: Akananuru 20: the friend, with the man listening unseen, says that on the town women's talk of a chariot on the dunes the mother has forbidden their shore play (அன்னை கடிகொண்டனளே). Kainnilai 52: the mother has kept the girl in (அன்னையும் இல்கடிந்தாள்), and the speaker asks whether to tell the man of the blame.
teaches: The long poem lets the man overhear the mother's ban, while the venba weighs telling him outright, so the pair shows the ban as the friend's lever for marriage, worked by indirection in one and nearly by open message in the other.

note: Kuruntokai 320: on the dune of drying fish and prawns she has not even one day's laughter with the shore lord to be blamed for, yet the town gossips. Kainnilai 54: on the same drying-ground he lied to her and enjoyed her beauty. On a plain reading one heroine denies what the other confesses.
teaches: The prawn-drying ground serves one heroine as the scene of an innocence the town will not credit and another as the scene of her seduction, so the stock place of neythal kalavu could carry either a defence before the town or an accusation of the lover.

note: Akananuru 20: the friend recalls chasing birds from her father's drying fish (எந்தை தந்த கொழுமீன் உணங்கல் படுபுள் ஓப்பி) among the shore pastimes now forbidden. Kainnilai 56: while driving the birds from the fish her kin brought (எமர் தந்த ... வன்மீன் கவரும்புள் ஓப்பின்), the shore lord took her beauty.
teaches: The same chore, keeping birds off the family's catch, is innocent play in the Akananuru list and the very hour of the theft in the venba, which explains why the mother's ban in the long poem falls on just those shore tasks.

note: Natrinai 138: the lord of the cool ford where the white heron lays its eggs (வெண் குருகு ஈனும் தண்ணம் துறைவன்) is now known to the old town. Kainnilai 59: the lord of the cool ford where the heron lays its eggs in the thaazhai (குருகுஈனும் தண்ணந் துறைவனை) is now known to the mother, who shuts the door.
teaches: The epithet of the nesting heron frames in both poems the moment the secret becomes known, to the town in one and the mother in the other, which supports reading the breeding heron as a call for the man to set up house now that kalavu is over.

note: Akananuru 315: the mother who saw the girl grow and suspected, yet did not shut her in (செறியேன்), mourns her elopement. Kainnilai 59: the mother, seeing the young man come through the gap, at once blocks it and shuts the door.
teaches: The confinement one mother blames herself for omitting is done at first sight by the other, and the friend reports it as the pressure that forces marriage, so the pair shows the mother's guard as the hinge between the two endings of kalavu, marriage and flight.

note: Kural 1157: do the bangles slipping from her wrist not already proclaim that the shore lord has left? Kainnilai 55: if the shore lord leaves without embracing her, the bangles will not stay on either hand.
teaches: The venba states as a condition what the couplet packs into a past tense, so it supports reading the Kural's 'has left' as anticipatory: the bangles slip at the mere prospect of the shore lord going.

note: Kural 1262: if she forgets him today her beauty will leave and her bangles slip. Kainnilai 58: if she sits thinking of him, her bangles will not hold. On a plain reading forgetting ruins her in one and remembering in the other.
teaches: The couplet makes memory the thing that keeps her body whole and the venba makes memory the thing that wastes it, so together they show the bangle as a sign the two traditions could hang on either side of remembering the absent man.

note: Ainkurunuru 200: the lord of the golden chariot has come, her bangles fit again and they can laugh at the pallor. Kainnilai 60: her golden pallor is gone, for here is the chariot of the man who saw the backs of fleeing kings, nearing Koodal.
teaches: Both mark the end of pallor by the chariot's arrival, but the venba arms the returning lover with a victor's epithet and the Pandya's Korkai and Koodal, showing a late akam poem borrowing puram glory to make homecoming a triumph.

note: Purananuru 369 (Paranar, thurai மறக்களவழி) builds the whole battle as a season of rain and tillage, elephants as clouds and arrows as rain on a wet field (ஈரச் செறுவயின்), ending in a request for elephants; Kalavazhi Narpathu 2 gives one farming image, blood running through burst drums like a tank's sluices after the monsoon (கார்ப்பெயல் பெய்தபின்).
teaches: Together they show how the kalavazhi theme changed form: Paranar's single sustained allegory of the farm year, made to earn a gift, becomes in Poigaiyar one quick water-and-field simile per stanza with no request, so the farming root of the genre's name survives only as a store of images.

note: Purananuru 19 (lines 8 to 9) likens arrows lodged in a wounded elephant to a flock of sparrows settled on a hill (குன்றத்து இறுத்த குரீஇஇனம் போல); Kalavazhi Narpathu 8 says elephants hidden by arrows look like countless hills with flocks of sparrows (எண்ணருங் குன்றிற் குரீஇயினம்).
teaches: The near-identical image shows a stock battle simile passing from a Pandya victory poem to a Chola one, and the frames show it carries no fixed feeling: in Purananuru 19 it leads into mothers weeping for sons and Death fleeing in shame, while in Poigaiyar it is pure spectacle of the victor's field.
audit_text_issue: KN 8 variant reading at line 2

note: Kural 597 holds up the elephant that plants its feet under a sheaf of arrows (புதையம்பிற் பட்டுப்பா டூன்றுங் களிறு) as the model of a mind that does not give way; Kalavazhi Narpathu 10 shows elephants pierced everywhere by arrows that cannot move and sink wearily where they stand (செல்கலா தொல்கி யுயங்கும்).
teaches: Seen from the battlefield, the Kural's emblem of steadfastness is ambiguous: the same arrow-struck elephant that stands its ground is, for the victor's poet, a beast too spent to move, so the maxim's courage depends on reading stillness as resolve rather than as defeat.

note: Purananuru 62 describes a battle in which both kings die, their drums are abandoned (முரசு ஒழிந்தனவே) and no one is left to claim the field (களங்கொளற்கு உரியோர் இன்றி); Kalavazhi Narpathu 11 describes the abandoned drums (ஒழிமுரசம்) of those whose strength failed, kicked by blinded elephants, on the field Sengan won.
teaches: The abandoned drum is the same sign in both, but whose drum it is decides what it means: when only the loser's drum is dropped it proves a victor and the field becomes his song, and when both drums fall, as in Purananuru 62, the field has no owner and the poet can only ask what the war was for.

note: Purananuru 373 (Kovur Kizhar, thurai மறக்களவழி) praises the Chola Killivalavan who made the Kongu turn their backs (கொங்கு புறம் பெற்ற) and ends among vultures on the fearful field, asking a gift; Kalavazhi Narpathu 14 names the Kongar as the enemy the lord of the river country killed (கொங்கரை அட்ட களத்து).
teaches: Read together they show that a Chola victory over the Kongu was already sung as a field-of-battle poem in the Purananuru, with the bard asking for his share; Poigaiyar keeps the enemy and the field but lets the stanza end on the field itself, turning a petition into a celebration complete without the bard's request.
audit_text_issue: Purananuru 373 lines 9, 13, 14, 18, 22, 23, 27, 32 are broken.

note: Kural 599, in the chapter on energy (ஊக்கமுடைமை), says the elephant, for all its bulk and sharp tusks, fears a tiger's attack; Kalavazhi Narpathu 16 shows horses, urged on (ஊக்கி) by picked warriors, leaping onto the elephants' brows like tigers springing up a hill.
teaches: The battle verse turns the Kural's animal fable into tactics: the tiger's assault on the elephant is what cavalry does to war elephants, so the couplet's claim that drive overcomes size had a familiar picture on the field, and Poigaiyar's simile names the driving force with the Kural's own word.
audit_text_issue: The packet's Kural 599 text has encoding junk (஦வ்ருஉம்) for வெரூஉம்.

note: Kalavazhi 36 sings the day the Kaveri lord took Kalumalam (கழுமலங் கொண்டநாள்), the enemy umbrellas overturned like mushrooms; Akananuru 44, a hero hurrying home after his king's war, names the Chola Senni who took Kalumalam and captured Kanaiyan (கணையன் அகப்படக் கழுமலம் தந்த) and likens the heroine to that king's rich town Kudavayil.
teaches: Kalavazhi leaves the loser at Kalumalam unnamed and shows only the carnage, while the akam poet names the captive Kanaiyan and spends the victory as a mark of the Chola's prosperity, so together they show one battle remembered both as a field of dead and as a byword for a well-kept land.

note: Kalavazhi 39 ends on the field where the Chola killed the Vanji king (வஞ்சிக்கோ), his white umbrella torn down and full of flesh; Purananuru 74 is a Chera king's own poem from captivity, held like a chained dog (தொடர்ப்படு ஞமலியின்) and begging water. The two are tied by the tradition that the Chera defeated in Kalavazhi was Kanaikkal Irumporai, the poet of Purananuru 74; neither text in our corpus states it.
teaches: The victor's song counts the Chera's defeat as the end of the matter, but the defeated king's poem says that being taken alive and fed by strangers is worse than the sword, so on that reading the field the Kalavazhi praises produced a fate its own frame cannot see.

note: Purananuru 19 has the cut-trunked elephants rolling on the ground like ploughs (நாஞ்சில் ஒப்ப நிலமிசைப் புரள) in a field where old mothers weep for their sons; Kalavazhi 40 has all the elephants fall as if the god of the silver plough (வெள்ளிவெண் ணாஞ்சிலான்) were ploughing the world.
teaches: The Purananuru simile sits beside the mothers' grief, while the Kalavazhi lifts the same plough image to a god's tillage and drops the mourners, showing how the battlefield-as-ploughing figure grew into a frame of pure praise once the kalavazhi became a genre of its own.

note: Purananuru 25 praises Chezhiyan because his spear stopped short when he saw the enemy's widows beat their breasts and cut their hair; Kalavazhi 29 shows the enemy's bereaved kin wailing in all four directions and closes on the Chola's field.
teaches: Both poets put the defeated side's mourners in a victory poem, but one makes the king's restraint before them the glory and the other makes their wailing part of the spectacle of the field, so the pair shows two incompatible uses of the same grief in royal praise.

note: Purananuru 62 describes a field where both kings fell, the umbrellas shook, the famous drums were lost and no one was left to claim the field (களங்கொளற்கு உரியோர் இன்றி); Kalavazhi 37 has the kings' corpses pour out blood that carries off the drums and the elephants, and the field belongs to the lord of the watered land.
teaches: The same lost drums and dead kings make a kalavazhi only because one king survives to own the field; Purananuru 62 shows the case where nobody does, and the poet must turn the praise to the heavenly guests, which marks the victor as the genre's precondition.

note: Kural 773 says fierceness is great manhood, but help given when misfortune befalls the foe is its cutting edge; Kalavazhi 35 ends with the enemy king falling with his royal elephant, struck like a lion on a thunder-struck mountain, and goes no further.
teaches: The Kural locates the height of valour in the moment after the foe falls, and the kalavazhi, built to stop at the field of killing, has no place for that moment, so the couplet names exactly what the battle-song leaves out.

note: Kural 774 praises the warrior who sends his spear off in an elephant and laughs as he plucks another from his own body; in Kalavazhi 23 the strong men (வயவர்) hurl and split the elephants' foreheads, and the field is Chempiyan's.
teaches: The Kural keeps the spear-thrower's own pride and wound in view, while the battle-song shows the same feat only through the speared elephants and credits it to the king, so the pair shows the warrior's deed moving from his ethic into his lord's fame.

note: Mullaippattu 1-6 likens the rain-cloud rising from the sea to Mal, who grew to measure the world; Kar Narpathu 1 likens the rainbow to the garland on the chest of Mal, coloured like the warring sea.
teaches: Both mullai poems open their rains with Mal, the god of the mullai land, so the land's god is the first image of its season; the later venba moves him from the rising cloud to the rainbow, making the sky his adorned chest rather than his growing body.

note: Akananuru 85: the friend tells the heroine not to weep, since the rain now spreading is the season he named when he assured them 'வருதும் யாம்'. Kar Narpathu 1 quotes the same promise, வருதும், and asks 'will he not come?'
teaches: The promise is the same word in both, which shows the friend's argument as a fixed form, quote his 'we shall come' and point to the rain, with the older poem supplying the peacock calling its mate as the proof the four-line verse leaves out.

note: In Mullaippattu the old women seeking an omen hear a herd girl tell the calves 'இன்னே வருகுவர் தாயர்' and take it as a sign; in Kar Narpathu 2 the lightning speaks his message, 'இன்னே வருவர் நமர்'.
teaches: The same formula of reassurance, 'they will come at once', is an overheard chance word in the idyll's omen rite and the sky's own message in the venba, so the later poem turns the ritual of listening for a sign into the season speaking for the absent man.

note: Both carry the same thurai, the friend showing the season to reassure the heroine, with the konrai in bloom; Akananuru 4 ends with his chariot in sight, Kar Narpathu 4 with the season as medicine for her pallor.
teaches: Set together they give two endings to one speech: the long poem can produce the man himself on the horizon, while the four-line venba has to stop at the season and so makes the season itself the cure.

note: Kar Narpathu 4: the season is the medicine for her pallor. Kural 1265: the pallor of her soft shoulders will leave only after she has seen her husband with full eyes; on a plain reading the two disagree about what cures pasalai.
teaches: The friend claims the sign of his return heals the pallor and the Kural's woman holds that only the sight of him will, so the couplet reads as the heroine's answer to the whole method of the Kar Narpathu's friend.

note: Kar Narpathu 5: he left fearing the words of those who scorn. Akananuru 111: the friend says he will come back, ashamed of the mocking words of hostile men (ஏஎச்சொல் நாணி).
teaches: Taken together, other men's contempt both sends the hero away for wealth and, in the friend's argument, drives him home again, so shame works on him at both ends of the journey.

note: Kural 1263: she lives on, longing for the return of the man who went desiring victory with his resolve as his only companion. Kar Narpathu 7: the friend says he went to give to seekers and crush foes, and the rain will bring him back.
teaches: The couplet's woman treats his heroic aim as the rival that left her behind, while the friend names the same aim, giving and conquest, as a reason to trust he will return in the rains: one motive is a grievance in the Kural and a guarantee in the venba.

note: Verse 7 gives the purpose of his journey as giving to seekers and destroying foes; verse 8 gives it as lasting fame in this earthly world.
teaches: Read in sequence, the friend's account of his motive moves from duties toward others to fame for himself while her proof stays the same rain-season sign, so the series varies the cause of absence and holds the cure fixed.

note: Kar Narpathu 9: the flowers speak many sweet words announcing his return. Akananuru 74: the heroine tells the friend she could hold firm on her many sweet words of reassurance (வன்புறை இன்சொல் நன்பல) were it not for the herders' flute at evening.
teaches: Akananuru 74 gives the heroine's answer that the Kar Narpathu never records: sweet words of comfort hold her only until the evening flute, so the reassurance the venbas repeat is shown elsewhere to fail at its own hour.

note: Akananuru 134: the returning hero tells the charioteer that if she hears the sound of the swift-horsed chariot (கடுமான் தேர்ஒலி) there may be union at midnight. Kar Narpathu 10: the friend hears the swift-horsed chariot coming like a forest stream and says the heroine will bloom.
teaches: The chariot's sound is the hinge of the reunion from both sides: the hero hopes she will hear it and the friend reports that it is heard and what it does to the heroine's body, in the same phrase கடுமான் தேர்.

note: Both liken the opening kodal cluster to a snake's raised hood in the rain-fed woodland; in Akananuru 154 the returning man sees it from the chariot, in Kar Narpathu 11 the friend points to it as the sign of his quick return.
teaches: The same flower-image is seen by the man on the road home and offered by the friend at home as a promise, so the shared stock of mullai images lets the two halves of a separation read the same sign in the same season.

note: Kar Narpathu 12: dark clouds like oiled elephants rise on the right every day, a sight beyond doubt that he will come. Mullaippattu 4-5: the cloud drinks the cold sea and rises rightward (வலனேர்பு), just before the old women go out to seek an omen.
teaches: The idyll sets the rightward-rising cloud beside a separate omen rite, while the venba makes the cloud itself the omen 'beyond doubt', which shows the rising on the right read as a good sign for the absent man's return.

note: Akananuru 9 ends with the returning man asking whether his heart, which went ahead longing for her soft shoulders, has reached her; Kar Narpathu 19 has the man say his heart has gone the long road wanting her as companion.
teaches: Both returning heroes speak of a heart that outruns the chariot, so the figure belongs to the set speech of return; the long poem follows the heart into the house and to her touch, while the venba stops at its setting out.

note: Akananuru 44: the king has finished his work, the enemy has paid tribute, and the man bids the charioteer drive ahead to sleep on his wife's breast. Kar Narpathu 20: the glorious king's work is done, the roads are pleasant, and the rain moves like an army.
teaches: Both make the king's finished war the condition of the husband's return, and the pair shows the venba compressing the long poem's catalogue of kings and battles into one simile in which the rain-cloud marches like the armies he leaves.

note: Kural 1268: let the king fight and win; let us join the house and keep the evening feast. Kar Narpathu 20: the king's work is finished, so the roads home are sweet.
teaches: The couplet is the wish spoken while the war goes on and the venba is the same man once it is granted, so read together they give the before and after of one situation, the hero held by the king's war until it ends.

note: Kuruntokai 240: the waiting woman sees mullai buds like a wild cat's teeth (வெருக்குப்பல் லுருவின் முல்லை) crowding the bush as the north wind comes and his hill sinks at evening. Kar Narpathu 21: the returning man sees the mullai buds pointed like the teeth of his girl.
teaches: The same bud-and-teeth simile becomes a predator's teeth for the waiting woman and the beloved's teeth for the returning man, so the mullai bud's meaning in these poems is set by which side of the separation is looking, not by the flower.

note: Both close with the same line, ஒண்டொடி யூடுநிலை. In 23 the friend shows the season to reassure; in 38, by the colophon, she concedes that he has lied.
teaches: One closing question about sulking serves first to dismiss the heroine's grievance (the season has come, so he will) and then to grant it (the season has come and he has not), so the series uses a formula line whose force is fixed only by the lines before it.

note: Akananuru 47: if we have finished the work here, rise quickly, heart (வினைஇவண் முடித்தனம் ஆயின்). Kar Narpathu 24: rise, heart, leaving all the work lying (எல்லா வினையுங் கிடப்ப). On a plain reading they disagree on whether the task must be done before he turns home.
teaches: The older poem holds the man's return behind the finishing of his task, while the venba's man drops the task once the rain and the memory of her hair reach him, so the same address to the heart sets duty and love in two different orders.

note: Both see the thonri open like a lamp in the rains: in Akananuru 235 (சுடர்கொள் அகலின்) the heroine asks whether he has forgotten them; in Kar Narpathu 26 (கார்த்திகை ... விளக்கிற்) the friend says the rain has come with his message.
teaches: The lamp-like thonri is evidence that he has forgotten for the heroine and evidence that he has sent word for the friend, so the one sign of the promised season can be read against him or for him depending on who speaks.

note: Kural 1187: she turned aside a little from his embrace and the pallor was on her thick enough to scoop up. Kar Narpathu 27: if we sulk that he left without a thought for us, pallor spreads over her in bed (பள்ளியுட் பாயும் பசப்பு).
teaches: The couplet's hyperbole, that the least turning away from him in bed brings pallor, becomes in the friend's mouth a practical warning against sulking at an absent man, so the venba shows the Kural's figure used as an argument for bearing up.

note: Kural 231: to give and live so that renown arises; there is no other gain for a life. Kar Narpathu 32: bees glad as the hearts of wealthy men who crave undying fame (கெடாஅப் புகழ்வேட்கைச் செல்வர் மனம்போற்).
teaches: The couplet states the craving for renown through giving as the one gain of life, and the venba treats that craving as so familiar that a returning lover can measure a bee's gladness by it, which shows the puram ideal already turned into common stock for akam imagery.

note: Ainkurunuru 447: may the king's work be released, and then we shall see her bright brow, when the bee opens the red thalavu bud shaped like a kingfisher's beak (சிரல்வாய்ச் செம்முகை). Kar Narpathu 36: the man returning from the work sees the thalavam buds, lovely as kingfishers' beaks (சிரல்வாய் வனப்பின), opened in rows.
teaches: The same thalavu bud is the hour hoped for in the man's prayer while the king's work holds him and the sight on the road once he is released, so read together the bud marks the two ends of a single wait.

note: Kar Narpathu 37: will our man, who took up the king's hard work, not come even in the season of great rains? Akananuru 304: in the king's war camp as the first rains fall, the man fears she will think him unkind, not knowing his pain.
teaches: The friend's confidence rests on the season alone, and the Akananuru shows that season from inside the king's camp, where the man is still held and can only dread her reproach, so the king's work she counts to his credit is the very thing keeping him away.

note: Akananuru 85: the friend says the cool rains, when the elephant feeds his young mate and calf with bamboo shoots, are the season he promised, so do not weep. Kar Narpathu 38: the bull elephant plays with his mate in the cool season, yet he has not come, and the colophon says the friend tells her he lied.
teaches: The elephant pair in the rains is the friend's proof of his promise in one poem and her proof of his breach in the other, so the creatures' act carries the same sense in both while the verdict on the man turns on whether he has come.

note: Natrinai 267: crabs of the sand dune with eyes like the nochchi's dark buds (நொச்சி மா அரும்பு அன்ன கண்ண). Kar Narpathu 39: nochchi buds opened like crabs' eyes (அலவன்க ணேய்ப்ப).
teaches: The simile runs in opposite directions: the neythal poem makes its shore crab the subject and borrows the nochchi as image, while the mullai venba makes its nochchi the subject and borrows the crab, so each poet takes the tenor from the poem's own land.

note: Both turn on the same words, செய்குறி வாரா ரவரென்று: in 25 the friend says that thought thickened the heroine's pallor; in 40 she says the darkening sky has become the medicine for the woman who grieved at it.
teaches: The series states one despairing thought twice, once as the cause of pallor in the friend's confession of her own distress and once as the sickness the sky now cures, so her speeches of despair and of comfort rest on the same premise and differ only in how they read the sky.

note: Thinaimalai 1 gives the man's question to the girls about a wounded beast (ஏமரை); Thinaimozhi 8 gives the friend's answer that no wounded tusker came this way.
teaches: Put together the two short books make one exchange, and the question's lavish praise of the girls' faces next to the friend's flat denial shows each side treating the wounded animal as a cover: he courts through it, and she refuses through it.

note: In 1 the man asks after the arrow-struck deer; in 9 he tells his companion that the asking after a beast was a ruse (வஞ்சமே) and that he was the one taken.
teaches: The book places the pretext and the confession apart, so 9 tells the reader how to read 1: the hunter's question was never about game, and the hunter who set out to deceive came back captured.

note: Ainthinai 14 has the friend say the man came 'like those who ask after a beast' (மாவினவு வார்போல) with something else to ask; Thinaimalai 9 has the man himself call his asking after a beast deceit.
teaches: The ruse is seen through from both sides, the friend naming it as a likeness and the hero confessing it as a trick, which shows the beast question as a convention both parties knew and played along with rather than a deception that worked.

note: In Akananuru 388 the girl, in private, mocks the diviner whose god is said to have caused her sickness; in Thinaimalai 12 the friend tells the household to send the velan away, free the kid and recognise the man who saved her from the flood.
teaches: The long poem stops at the girl's private scorn for the rite, and the short one shows the next move, so the pair shows mockery of the velan turning into the friend's disclosure to the family, where dismissing the diviner and naming the rescuer are one act.

note: 12 says the girl will give her shoulders only to the man who swam the flood and set her on the bank; 14 says no one but the man who drove off the elephant shall touch her friend's shoulders. Both use the same 'except him, no one' formula.
teaches: The same exclusive formula is fitted to two different rescues, flood and elephant, which shows that the rescue is an interchangeable warrant and that what the friend really presents to the household is the girl's choice, already made.

note: 2 tells of the man who dressed the girl's hair with flowers and drove off the musth elephant from the platform; 14 tells of the elephant driven off and concludes that no one but him shall touch her shoulders.
teaches: Read in order, 2 lays out the evidence (the flowers in her hair, the rescue) and 14 draws the verdict, so the disclosure to the household is built like a case: first the facts, then the right those facts give him.

note: Kural 1131 says that for those who suffer in love there is no safeguard and strength but the palmyra horse; in Thinaimalai 16 the man stands on the madal in the street and will not leave until she grants him her breast.
teaches: The couplet names the madal as the lover's only strength in general terms, and the quatrain shows what that strength is in use: a public siege in the street with a single stated condition and no second way, so the 'safeguard' is pressure on her household, not comfort for him.

note: Kural 1085 has the man at first sight find in her look Death, an eye and a doe; Thinaimalai 8 has the man at the fields find Kaman's arrows, five twice over, in the girl's two eyes.
teaches: Both men read a killing power in the first look, but the Kural names it Death while the field poem gives it to the love god and counts the arrows, which shows the same wound drawn once as mortal danger and once as a wound meant to be healed in union.

note: In Natrinai 300 a suitor sets a great chariot at the gate as the price of the girl's bangles (சிறு வளை விலை); in Thinaimalai 15 the friend says no price, not the sea-girt world, could buy the girl, and she must be given to the elders who come for her.
teaches: Natrinai shows a bride price actually offered, and Thinaimalai answers the practice: by declaring her beyond any price the friend moves the marriage from purchase to gift, so the only claim the household should honour is the formal coming of the suitor's elders.

note: Akananuru 18 says that if the man suffers harm on the night ford even once, her friend will not live after it, and asks him to come by day; Thinaimalai 7 says that if he comes by night the daughter of the hill lord will not live.
teaches: Thinaimalai's flat 'she will not live' is explained by Akananuru 18: her life hangs on his safety on the path, so forbidding the night visit protects her through him, and the long poem's offer of a daytime meeting shows what the short ban leaves for him to infer.

note: Thinaimozhi 2 says the guarding of the millet fields has ended and asks whether his coming will now be hard; Thinaimalai 5 says the millet has ripened like the fruit of past deeds and that this parts them.
teaches: Thinaimozhi gives the harvest as a fact of the field, and Thinaimalai frames the same harvest as the ripening of deeds into their fruit, which turns the end of the meetings from a farming date into something like fate, and so adds weight to the push for marriage.

note: Both men fear the girl's waist will break: the Kural through the flowers' stems, Thinaimalai 17 if she walks even a little.
teaches: The Kural keeps the snapping waist a joke of praise, a mock funeral drum, while Thinaimalai 17 lets the same fear spill into the man's own body, whose heart sways wherever she sways, so the conceit of her fragility becomes a measure of his surrender.

note: Thinaimalai 18 fears that the harvested millet ends the bond; in Akananuru 132 the millet ears are already cut and the friend tells the man to take the girl away.
teaches: Thinaimalai 18 stops at the fear that the stubble field ends the meetings, and Akananuru 132 shows what the friend does with that fear, turning it into a demand to take the girl away, so the harvest is the point at which kalavu must become marriage or flight.

note: The Kural's man asks whether her look is Death; the man of Thinaimalai 22 says her two eyes shot him as her brothers shoot beasts.
teaches: The Kural names the killing look in the abstract, and Thinaimalai 22 grounds it in her people's trade, measuring her two eyes against her brothers' single killing arrow, so the deadly glance of the couplet turns out to be a hunter's weapon of the hills.

note: Natrinai 13 likens the girl's red-lined eyes to the arrows millet-watchers pull out of a felled beast; Thinaimalai 22 has her eyes as two arrows that have felled the man.
teaches: The friend of Natrinai 13 gives the eyes the hunters' bloodied arrows, and the man of Thinaimalai 22 draws the consequence that he is the beast they brought down, so the two poems together show the eye-as-arrow belonging to a hunting household's daily kill.

note: Both use the formula of the kin who cut and plough (எறிந்து உழுது, எறிந்தெமர் தாம்உழுத); in Ainthinai Aimpathu 18 it is the field they cleared, in Thinaimalai 24 a sign of their hardness.
teaches: In Ainthinai Aimpathu 18 clearing and ploughing is just the kin's labour whose harvest ends the meetings, but Thinaimalai 24 reads the same labour as a temperament, men who fell fragrance for grain, so the friend can turn the hill family's farming into a reason the girl will not pity the man.

note: Both show an elephant that has escaped the curve-striped tiger; in Ainthinai Aimpathu 16 it lies hurt on the hero's night path, in Thinaimalai 25 it is the likeness of the trembling girl.
teaches: Ainthinai Aimpathu 16 puts the escaped elephant on the man's path as a danger the sleepless girl imagines, and Thinaimalai 25 makes the escaped elephant the girl herself, still shaking after the danger, so one stock scene can stand either for the night road or for the fear it leaves in her.

note: In both the fallen vengai flowers look like a tiger: in Akananuru 228 a she-elephant bolts from them on the man's moonlit way home, in Thinaimalai 26 the girl will not survive his night visit.
teaches: Akananuru 228 shows the vengai's false tiger frightening a beast on the path, and Thinaimalai 26 transfers that fright to the waiting girl, which shows that the friend's case against the night visit rests on fear of a likeness rather than on any real tiger.

note: In Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 10 the girl tells her friend that mother, learning of the union, has barred her from the field; in Thinaimalai 27 the friend tells the man that mother saw him and keeps the girl guarded.
teaches: The same discovery by the mother is grief in the girl's mouth, who wonders whether he will be vexed, and a lever in the friend's, who uses it to tell him to marry now, so the confinement that ends kalavu is also the friend's strongest argument for marriage.
audit_text_issue: Thinaimalai 27 line 2-3 'முனிவரையுள் நின்றான் வலியாக' is obscure.

note: Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 5 warns the man off because the kin carry bows, spears and swift arrows; Thinaimalai 28 warns him through the precious trees the kin cut down to plough.
teaches: Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 5 states the threat as weapons, and Thinaimalai 28 leaves weapons out and lets the felled sandal and agil show what the brothers would do to an intruder, so the threat can be carried by how a family treats its own hill rather than by its arms.

note: Akananuru 92 forbids the night and promises the man a day meeting by a cool fall where red glory lilies open; Thinaimalai 29 describes such a place by a forest stream in a glory-lily thicket.
teaches: Akananuru 92 gives the day tryst as the friend's offer in exchange for the dangerous night, and Thinaimalai 29 gives only the place, which shows the daytime meeting ground was a fixed set (stream, glory lilies, low shade) a four-line verse could call up without the bargain around it.
audit_text_issue: Thinaimalai 29 line 1 is missing from the comparison site text.

note: Both turn on the leaf-garment and the pun on வேங்கை (kino tree and tiger); in 20 the tigers are the girl's brothers and mother and the gift is refused, in 31 the tiger is the man himself and his gift is praised.
teaches: Read together, the friend moves the tiger from the girl's family to her lover as she moves from turning the leaf-garment away to pressing the girl toward him, so the same pun marks which side of the courtship holds the danger at each stage.

note: Kural 1085 finds death, an eye and a doe in the young woman's look; Thinaimalai 32 calls the fish-guard's long eyes a weapon (படைநெடுங்கண்) whose guarding falls on the man.
teaches: The couplet lists in the abstract what a first look can be, and the poem supplies the scene that makes 'death' concrete: a girl posted to guard the drying fish whose watch is turned on the man who looks, so the Kural's killing glance is a guard's weapon.
audit_text_issue: Line 4 'கடிபொல்லா' is hard.

note: 32 is the man's first sight of the girl guarding the drying fish; 44 has the friend name the grove of that same task as the girl's place.
teaches: Read together the two verses show the fish-drying watch doing for the neythal girl what the millet watch does in kurinji: it is where the man first sees her and, later, the daytime meeting place the friend appoints.

note: Akananuru 80: the friend says they spend the day driving birds from their father's drying fish and bids him come by day to the punnai grove; Thinaimalai 44 names the grove where the girl went to drive birds from the drying fish (புட்கடிவான் புக்க).
teaches: The long poem spells out the trade behind the short one: naming the grove where the girl chases birds from the fish is the friend's way of replacing the dangerous night swim with a day meeting, which Thinaimalai 44 implies but never states.

note: Akananuru 80 forbids the night swim and offers a day meeting in the punnai grove; Thinaimalai 35 forbids the night and warns that a day visit brings gossip.
teaches: Set beside Akananuru 80, where the day meeting is the friend's remedy for the night's danger, Thinaimalai 35 shows a later stage in which the day too is closed by gossip, so that the only road left is marriage.
audit_text_issue: site prints a different verse 35; சுலா அகற்றி, மார்க் obscure

note: Both use a shore bird that takes something else for a heron's chick: in Ainkurunuru 151 a stork treads a neythal flower going to see it; in Thinaimalai 36 a heron feeds a screwpine bud and shades it with its wings.
teaches: The same mistake of a bird taking a flower for a chick can carry opposite senses: in Ainkurunuru the error bruises the flower, which still gives off scent, like the heroine who stays tender to the man who hurt her, while in Thinaimalai it becomes devoted care held up to shame a man whose visits do not stay.

note: Kuruntokai 25: no one but the man was there, only a heron watching for fish, on the day he took her; Thinaimalai 37: the tide knew it that day (ஓதநீர் அன்றறியும்), so marry her before the common square.
teaches: Kuruntokai's girl fears that a union witnessed only by a shore creature leaves her helpless if he lies, and Thinaimalai's friend answers that fear: a witness that cannot speak is why the union must be made public in the square.

note: Kuruntokai 163 asks the sea who has afflicted it (யாரணங் குற்றனை) since she hears it even at midnight; Thinaimalai 38 asks the sleepless sea who did this to it, 'like me'.
teaches: Kuruntokai leaves the girl's own state unsaid behind her question to the sea, while Thinaimalai 38 names it, the breast of the shore lord and a sleeplessness 'like mine', so the pair shows the later poet making explicit the projection the older poem left to the hearer.

note: In Akananuru 380 the man shows the girls a crab carrying a naaval fruit to its mate and says 'this is a fine way'; in Thinaimalai 40 the girl watches a crab playing with its mate after the man has left.
teaches: The crab with its mate is the shore lover's own emblem of devotion, used by the man in Akananuru 380 to court the girl; Thinaimalai 40 shows the emblem turned against him, watched by the girl alone after he dismissed her ache and went.

note: Kural 1147: the sickness grows with the town's gossip as manure and the mother's words as water; Thinaimalai 41: the heart melts day after day while the talk swells, like a storm cloud pouring.
teaches: The Kural makes the gossip the food of the love-sickness, and Thinaimalai 41 makes the two one weather, the swelling talk and the melting heart pouring together like a cloud, which shows the girl suffering the growth the couplet describes as a cause.

note: In Natrinai 287 the girl says he came unafraid of the dread crocodile of the backwater; in Thinaimalai 46 the friend bars him from the night when the striking shark circles.
teaches: The night beast of the backwater counts for the girl in Natrinai 287 as the proof of his love and for the friend in Thinaimalai 46 as the reason to stop him and ask for marriage, so the same danger is read by each speaker to serve her own aim.

note: Kural 1081: the man cannot tell whether she is a goddess (அணங்கு), a peahen or a woman; Thinaimalai 47: she is a beauty that strikes like a goddess (ஏரணங்கு) those who look without thinking.
teaches: The Kural's man hesitates over what she is, while the Thinaimalai speaker has settled it and turns to blame, saying her kin have let such a danger loose unguarded, so the pair shows the first-sight wonder of the couplet hardening into a lover's complaint.
audit_text_issue: Line 3 'சாவார்சான் றாண்மை சலித்திலா' is obscure.

note: 48 describes the pearl-lit village at nightfall with no hearer; 49 addresses the shore lord with the same pearls dispelling the midnight dark and asks where he will come.
teaches: Read together, the bare description of 48 gains its speech act from 49: the pearl-light that seems praise of the shore's riches is the friend's ground for refusing the night tryst.

note: Akananuru 80: the friend says he has come by night across the dark backwater of crocodiles and sharks and asks him to come by day to the grove where they guard drying fish. Thinaimalai 49: no dark at all to cross, since the pearls sweep away the midnight.
teaches: The two friends refuse the same night visit for opposite reasons, the older one because the dark hides beasts and the venba because the shore has no dark to hide him, so the convention needs only the refusal and lets the reason be turned inside out.
audit_text_issue: Thinaimalai 49 line 3 'நரன்யியிர்த்த' looks corrupt

note: 50 sets the hero's stealthy coming, like sleep and without a tryst, against the proper way; 52, with the same shore-army image, names the proper way: choose a day and marry.
teaches: The vague நெறியால் of 50 is spelled out in 52 as நாள் ஆய்ந்து வரைதல், so the sequence moves from forbidding the secret visit to prescribing the rite, with the marshalled shore as the model of order in both.

note: 52: the shore is like a king who rises without haste, so fix a day. 53: the shore is like a king who has risen and will not settle, so come before our kin move.
teaches: One image of the shore as a royal army is given opposite tempos, unhurried and restless, to argue first for deliberation and then for urgency, which shows the poet using the image to set the pace of the plea rather than to carry a fixed sense.
