note: Purananuru 42: the Chola's army roars like the sea. Thinaimalai 52: the sea, with waves for mahouts and boats for elephants, is like a king's force rising.
teaches: The puram simile is run backwards in the neythal venba: where the war poem makes an army sound like the sea, the love poem makes the sea a mustered army, so that the shore lord is held to a king's measured conduct and the wedding becomes his orderly campaign.

note: Natrinai 45: the friend tells the rich man's son that they are fishermen's daughters who drive birds from drying shark and smell of fish (புலவு நாறுதும்), so their life is no match for his. Thinaimalai 51: we watch and sell the fish on the sand that reeks of it.
teaches: The venba keeps only the smell and the trade and drops the explicit 'go away, we are not your equals' of the Natrinai, which shows how far the later poet could rely on the reader supplying the refusal from the fish-smell alone.

note: Akananuru 80: the friend tells the shore lord that they guard their father's drying fish from birds in the punnai grove and asks him to come there by day. Thinaimalai 51: we watch and sell the fish in the grove.
teaches: The same chore that in Natrinai 45 marks the girls as beneath the suitor is in Akananuru 80 the cover for a daytime meeting, so the venba's bare picture of fish-watching could be either a rebuff or an invitation, which is why its sense stays open.

note: Akananuru 86: the husband recalls the wedding held at a bright dawn when the moon stood free of the evil planet on a faultless day. Thinaimalai 54: the friend tells the hero to call the diviners and choose a day.
teaches: The diviners' day that the friend demands in the venba is the day the older poem remembers by the moon's freedom from the planet, so the pair shows the omen-reading as the hinge that turns the secret tryst into the public rite.

note: Natrinai 303: the heroine lies sleepless at each cry of the anril joined with its mate in the palmyra of the common ground. Thinaimalai 56: the friend tells the shore lord that the anril calls from the tall palmyras of their front yard.
teaches: Natrinai 303 shows what the anril's cry does to the heroine at midnight, so when the friend in the venba points the hero to the anril in their own yard she is telling him, without saying so, what the girl hears each night he is away.

note: Kalittokai 124: the white waves ring the white dune like the blue garment worn by the milk-white elder brother of the god who measured the world. Thinaimalai 58: the dark sea and the white sand lie together like Mayavan and his elder brother.
teaches: Both neythal poets read the shore's dark and white through the two divine brothers, but Kalittokai puts both colours on the one white brother in his blue cloth, while the venba splits them between the two brothers, so the sea and the sand become kin rather than body and garment.

note: Kuruntokai 217: the friend tells the hill lord that meeting by day is possible while they guard the millet, but she fears his coming by night. Thinaimalai 59: by day the gossip is great, and by night the dangers are as great.
teaches: The Kuruntokai friend still leaves the day open and fears only the night, while the venba's friend closes both, so the pair shows the second step of the convention, where barring day and night together leaves marriage as the only way.

note: Kural 1081: on first seeing her the man cannot tell whether she is a goddess, a peahen or a woman, and his heart reels (மாலும்). Thinaimalai 60: the hero names the long-eyed girl plucking neythal as the fisherman's daughter who has made him mad (மையல்).
teaches: The couplet's lover reels because he cannot tell what she is, while the venba's lover knows exactly who she is, a fisherman's daughter at the shore, and is mad all the same, so the scene shows the bewilderment surviving the answer to the Kural's question.

note: Kural 101: for help given unasked, earth and heaven together are hardly a return. Thinaimalai 62: no one on this sea-girt earth matches the shore lord who once helped in the salt land; seek his equal in heaven.
teaches: The venba takes the Kural's measure of unrequited help, earth and heaven, and applies it to the helper himself: the lover's one service makes him without equal in either world, so the ethical rule of gratitude becomes the friend's argument for the man.

note: Kalittokai 33: in spring the silk-cotton flowers like fire and the pungu sheds blossom like puffed rice (எரி உரு உறழ இலவம், பொரி உரு உறழப் புன்கு), and the heroine feels the season mock the lonely. Thinaimalai 64 gives the murukku as scattered fire and the pungu as scattered puffed rice.
teaches: The pungu as puffed rice is fixed across both poems while the fire moves from silk-cotton to murukku, and the same paired images serve the heroine's complaint in Kalittokai and the friend's rebuke of open grieving in the venba, so the spring catalogue was a shared stock that either speaker could turn.
audit_text_issue: thinaimalai_nootraimpathu:64: நாணிண்மை read as நாண் இன்மை; the speaker's purpose turns on it.

note: Akananuru 369: the foster mother grieves that since the girl left, the parrot will not drink its milk, her playmates do not play and the doll gets no offering. Thinaimalai 73: the mother says the girl has given up her playmates' parrot and the pond's blue lily.
teaches: Read together they give both sides of the break: in the Akananuru the home's things go without the girl, in the venba the girl has already let go of the things her beauty was measured by, so the mother's grief covers both what the house lost and what the daughter chose.

note: Kalittokai 11: the heroine reasons that the man will return because he told her the burning forest holds a tusker that lets its mate drink the little muddy water first, a dove that fans its mate and a stag that shades its doe. Thinaimalai 78: an elephant alone finds no water in the spring and falls.
teaches: The same waterless road gives comfort in Kalittokai 11 and fear in the venba, and the difference is whether the poet gives the elephant a mate: the paired beast turns drought into proof of tenderness, the lone beast only into a measure of danger.

note: Kalittokai 11 closes its argument that the man will return with the omens at home: the lizard chirps on the good side and her lovely eye throbs on the left (உண் கண்ணும் ஆடுமால், இடனே). Thinaimalai 80 ends on the same left-eye omen, with the same closing word இடம்.
teaches: Kalittokai 11 reaches the throbbing left eye only after a long proof from the man's own words, while the venba rests the promise of return on the omen alone, which shows the left-eye sign was a recognised closing proof that could carry a whole short poem.

note: Kuruntokai 135: the friend tells the heroine not to cry: the man himself said work is life to men and men are life to women of the house, so he will put off his going. Thinaimalai 82: the friend says a man's duty makes him go for wealth, so she should not grieve. On the plain reading the two friends draw opposite conclusions from the same premise.
teaches: Both friends begin from the maxim that work belongs to men, but the Kuruntokai adds that men are women's life and concludes he will stay, while the venba stops at the man's duty and concludes he will go, so the outcome turns entirely on whether the maxim's second half is said.

note: Purananuru 312 assigns each person a கடன்: bearing the son is the mother's, making him worthy the father's, and killing elephants in battle the young man's. Thinaimalai 82 calls going to make wealth the man's கடன், repeating the word three times.
teaches: The venba carries the heroic vocabulary of duty from the battlefield to the trade road: what Purananuru 312 makes the young man's duty in war, the later akam friend makes his duty in wealth-making, and uses it to silence the wife's grief.

note: Akananuru 375: the heroine says she would not weep if she knew he passed unharmed the waste where raw youths kill even travellers without ornaments to test their arrows. Thinaimalai 84: the same robbers who shoot travellers with no wealth are the heroine's reason he should not go at all.
teaches: The robbers who kill the penniless serve the Akananuru heroine as a fear for a man already on the road and the venba's heroine as an argument against his setting out, so one road-danger supports both the anxiety after departure and the plea before it.

note: Kalittokai 15 ends a long plea with the argument that wealth can be made any day, but asks whether it can bring back youth once it has passed (வளமையோ வைகலும் செயல் ஆகும் ... இளமையும் தருவதோ). Thinaimalai 85 builds its whole verse on the same contrast of வளமை and இளமை.
teaches: The venba condenses into four lines the closing move of a long Kalittokai paalai, keeping even the rhyme of வளமை and இளமை, which shows that the retort had become a fixed argument of the separation poem that needed no road scene to carry it.

note: Naladiyar 11: knowing grey hair will come, the wise renounce in childhood, while those who delight in fleeting youth rise later on a staff. Thinaimalai 85: because youth cannot be brought back, the man should stay with his wife rather than chase wealth. On a plain reading the same fact counsels withdrawal in one and staying for love in the other.
teaches: From the one premise that youth does not return, the Naladiyar argues for leaving pleasure early and the paalai friend for keeping it while it lasts, so the impermanence of youth was an argument that served the householder's love as readily as the renouncer's flight.

note: Kural 1151: if you are not leaving, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will still be alive. Thinaimalai 86: told that he will surely go, the heroine says to name anyone who could bear it.
teaches: Both meet the news of his going by sending the message elsewhere, to whoever can survive it, and the venba supplies the starving elephant's waste that the couplet leaves out, so the Kural's bare retort is shown to be the stock reply of the paalai heroine to the announcement of departure.

note: Kalittokai 9: the mother asks travelling brahmins whether they saw her daughter and the youth; they say they did, and argue that as sandal, pearl and music serve others than their source, so the daughter belongs to the man she followed. Thinaimalai 89: travellers say they saw the man like the sun and the girl like the moon.
teaches: The venba keeps Kalittokai 9's frame of the mother questioning travellers and their 'we saw them' but drops the brahmins' argument that a daughter belongs to her husband, so the consolation shrinks to an image of a well-matched pair, and the mother is left with a report rather than a reason.

note: Kuruntokai 315: the heroine says the hill man is like the sun (ஞாயிறு அனையன்) and her shoulders like the nerunji flower. Thinaimalai 89: the man is like the hot sun and the girl like the cool moon.
teaches: In the Kuruntokai the man as sun makes the woman a nerunji that turns after him, while in the venba she is the moon, a second light of her own, so the same sun-image yields dependence in one poem and parity in the other.
audit_text_issue: Thinaimalai 89 line 2 is read only tentatively.

note: Akananuru 195: the mother of the eloped girl, after picturing the other mother preparing her house for the couple, asks the diviner whether the youth will bring the girl first to her house or take her to his own (எம்மனை முந்துறத் தருமோ? தன்மனை உய்க்குமோ?). Thinaimalai 90 asks the same question in nearly the same words.
teaches: The venba keeps the Akananuru mother's question almost word for word while dropping the rival mother's preparations and her own years of nursing, which shows that by the later anthology the question to the diviner had become a fixed turn of the eloped girl's mother that could stand without its reasons.

note: Kural 1230: thinking of the man whose nature is wealth, in this bewildering evening (மருள்மாலை) my life that would not die is dying. Thinaimalai 94: in the bewildering evening (மருள்மாலை), when the moon pours a false day, my life does not stay within but rides away.
teaches: The venba takes the couplet's own phrase for the hour and adds the cause the couplet leaves out, a moon that fakes daylight, so the bewilderment of the evening becomes a trick of the sky rather than only a state of her mind.

note: Kural 1221: you are not evening but வேலை, the time that eats the life of the once-wed. Thinaimalai 96: the dark like Maayon's colour and the milk-white moonlight are like a spear (வேல்) to those without a partner.
teaches: The Kural's pun on வேலை (hour, and the sense that kills) is made literal in the venba as a spear, and it moves from the evening to the moonlit night, showing a later poet turning the couplet's wordplay into a simile.

note: Kar Narpathu 19: the returning man sees the maraa blossom white like the plough-bearing god's colour and his heart runs ahead. Thinaimalai 96: the moonlight is like the pale colour of the discus-bearer's elder brother and falls like a spear on the parted.
teaches: Balarama's whiteness is a stock likeness in the Kilkanakku mullai poems, but it serves the hurrying man as the colour of the flowers that call him home and the waiting woman as the colour of a moonlight that wounds her, so the same divine colour signs joy or pain by who sees it.

note: Kural 1224: when the lover is away, evening comes like enemies coming to a killing ground. Thinaimalai 97: the sun sets like the discus Maayavan hurled at his foes' elephant, and she cannot bear the evening.
teaches: Both make evening a killing, but the couplet gives the killers no face while the venba names them through the land's own god, so the waiting woman of the mullai sees her evening through the war myth of the god of her own landscape.
audit_text_issue: line 2 வாழிபோல் must be read as ஆழி for the discus; பாழிபோல் unfixed

note: Kuruntokai 148: konrai buds like the gold coins of rich children's anklets bloom with the kurunthu; if you say this is not the rainy season, is it a dream? Thinaimalai 98: the konrai blooms into anklet, golden coin, garland and more; look at it now, you and the others.
teaches: Kuruntokai uses the anklet-coin likeness to make the konrai unanswerable evidence that the season has come, and the venba expands that single likeness into a run of six ornament shapes and calls witnesses, so the flowering becomes a proof displayed to an audience.

note: Kural 1261: my eyes have lost their lustre (வாளற்று) and my fingers are worn from counting the days since he left. Thinaimalai 99: like my lustre, my eyes have lost their light (வாள் இழந்த), my shoulders their beauty, my soft fingers worn with counting the days.
teaches: The venba keeps the couplet's two proofs of waiting, dim eyes and worn fingers, but sets them as a retort to a friend who called the grief idle (வாளா), so the Kural's private lament is turned into evidence in an argument.

note: Kar Narpathu 25: the flowers have opened; at the thought that the signs he set have come and he has not, the pallor has thickened on her. Thinaimalai 100: the rains appear in all quarters, his chariot does not, pallor appears and tears appear.
teaches: Kar Narpathu's friend reports the pallor from outside as a result of a broken sign, while the Thinaimalai woman lays it out as one sequence of appearings that begins with his false word, so the same symptom is shown first as a diagnosis and then as an accusation.

note: Kural 1185: look there, my lover goes; look here, the pallor spreads on my body. Thinaimalai 100: the rains appear, the lover's chariot does not, the pallor appears.
teaches: The couplet times the pallor to his leaving and the venba times it to his failure to return, so the two together show pallor at both ends of the absence, first as its shadow and then as its proof.

note: Kural 1269: for those who long for the day of the far one's return, one day passes like seven. Thinaimalai 101: since the man of the decorated chariot went, only the days on which he does not come keep coming.
teaches: The couplet stretches each day of waiting while the venba empties the calendar of the one day she waits for, so together they show waiting as both a lengthening of days and an endless supply of the wrong ones.

note: Kar Narpathu 38: even in this cool season, when the bull elephant plays with his mate, he has not come; why sulk? Thinaimalai 102: the deer everywhere play with their does, and I, not judging his going a harm, have paid my life for it.
teaches: In Kar Narpathu the friend uses the playing pair against the absent man and against the woman's sulk, while in Thinaimalai the woman reads the playing deer against herself, so the same sign of paired beasts can be turned to blame him or to blame her own consent.

note: Kuruntokai 148: if you say this is not the rainy season (காரன்று என்றி), is this a dream? Thinaimalai 103: you say the season has not come (பருவந்தான் பட்டின்றே என்றி); with tears I have cooked my life for it.
teaches: Both women quote the friend's denial of the season with the same என்றி, but the Kuruntokai woman answers with the evidence of the flowers and the Thinaimalai woman with the cost to her life, so the reply moves from disputing the fact to declaring the dispute too late.

note: Kuruntokai 382: the friend says the rain is unseasonable (வம்பு); if this were the true season, would he not come? Thinaimalai 103: to the friend who says the rain is unripe and the season not yet come, the woman says she has already wasted her life in tears.
teaches: Kuruntokai gives the friend's consolation in full and lets it stand, and the Thinaimalai venba shows it being received and failing, so the pair shows the stock argument of the false season from both the side that offers it and the side it does not reach.

note: Kuruntokai 66: the friend says the konrai are foolish (மடவ) to take the stray rain for the season and bloom. Thinaimalai 104: the woman says the konrai, blooming at the cloud's word, has killed her (கொன்றாய்).
teaches: On the friend's reading the konrai's early flowering is a harmless mistake that proves nothing, and on the woman's it is a killing, so the same tree judged foolish in the consolation is judged guilty by the one it was meant to console.
audit_text_issue: Thinaimalai 104 line 2 இந்துருவின் obscure.

note: Kuruntokai 290: do those who tell me to bear my love not know what it is, or are they so strong? Thinaimalai 106: who are they who tell the parted to bear it? They are so only for themselves, for the bees already sing in the mullai.
teaches: Kuruntokai answers the counsel to endure by doubting the counsellors' knowledge, while the venba adds the season's evidence against it, the bees already singing in joy, so the refusal to bear up gains in the later poem a reason drawn from the landscape.

note: Kar Narpathu 11: the kodal puts out clusters like the raised heads of snakes, and the scrub announces his quick return. Thinaimalai 107: the kodal, fearing the kaayaa as peacocks, shrinks, and the cloud like a five-headed snake falls on my head.
teaches: Kar Narpathu uses the snake-headed kodal as a happy sign of his return, and Thinaimalai keeps the snake likeness but lets it run on into the logic of snake and peacock, so the same image that comforted the waiting woman becomes a fable of fear.

note: Kuruntokai 183: the great flowering branch of the kaayaa shows like a peacock's neck in the poor forest. Thinaimalai 107: the kodal fears the budding kaayaa as a flock of peacocks.
teaches: The kaayaa-peacock likeness that Kuruntokai offers as the poet's own comparison is in Thinaimalai mistaken by a flower in the scene, so the later poet makes a stock simile into an error committed inside the landscape.

note: In Natrinai 246 the friend sees the golden konrai and the rumbling sky and says this is the season he named, so he will come; in 109 the heroine sees the same konrai under the sea-fed clouds and says he will not appear.
teaches: The same golden konrai is read as proof of return by the friend and as proof of desertion by the heroine, which shows that the flower settles nothing by itself: it only fixes the day by which his failure becomes certain.

note: In Kural 1222 the parted woman pities the dim evening as a sufferer like herself; in 110 the hills weep in pity for her while the wild jasmine laughs.
teaches: The Kural lets the woman lend her grief to one hour of the day, while the quatrain divides the whole landscape into those who mock her and those who mourn with her, so the pathetic projection becomes a judgment on which things are great.

note: Kar Narpathu 4: peacocks like dancing women, the konrai in bloom and humming bees make this season the medicine for her pallor, says the friend; 111: the forest as a stage, the bees as lute and the peacock dancing make the heroine ask how to survive.
teaches: Set side by side, the two show that the rainy-season pageant had two fixed readings, the friend's cure and the heroine's ordeal, and that the dancing peacock and humming bees are the same evidence in both: what differs is whether one trusts the promise.

note: Akananuru 82 makes the hill a stage with bamboo flute, waterfall drum, bee lute and peacock dancer, ending in the heroine alone with tear-filled eyes; 111 rebuilds the stage in the rain-forest with the glory lily's hands, the sky's call and the bee lute.
teaches: Moved from the kurinji hill to the mullai forest, the nature-theatre keeps its function of tormenting the lone woman but changes its occasion, from the lover seen by many in secret love to the season of a husband's promised return.

note: Kural 1228: the herdsman's flute, herald of the burning evening, kills like a weapon; 112: at sunset the sweet flute turns hot, and the friend answers that he will not fail and they must stand ready to receive him.
teaches: The Kural stops at the killing flute, while the quatrain gives the friend's reply to that very hour, turning the evening's heat into the household's readiness for a guest, so the flute is shown to be a test of trust as well as a pain.

note: Kuruntokai 66: the konrai is foolish, blooming on a stray rain before the season he named; 114: the kurundham blooms before the clouds have even shed their drops, and the heroine says it has fixed the season and decreed her grief.
teaches: The premature bloom that the Kuruntokai friend waves away as a plant's mistake is, to the heroine of 114, a verdict, which shows that the consolation of untimely rain only works on someone who does not take the flower as the sign itself.
audit_text_issue: 114 lines 1-2 (பாத்துப் படுகடல் ... காத்து) are hard to construe. | Thinaimalai 114 line 1 is hard to construe; the marker flagged the sense.

note: Kar Narpathu 21: the returning man sees the small mullai buds pointed like the girl's teeth; 116: the friend tells the mullai and its companions that their tooth-white buds have made the girl pale.
teaches: The bud that looks like her teeth is a pleasure on the road home and a wound in the waiting house, so the image's sense depends on whether the man is coming: the same likeness that recalls her smile to him drains her colour while he is away.

note: Kar Narpathu 10: the thunder roars and the herd bull bellows back at it, and the chariot comes so her body will freshen; 117: the thunder rages, the rutting elephant trumpets back and the cobra hides, and her shoulders pale.
teaches: In both the beast answering the thunder marks the height of the rains, and the pair shows that this moment is the hinge of the mullai wait: with the chariot heard it brings her colour back, and without it the same roar is when the pallor sets in.
audit_text_issue: Thinaimalai 117 line 3 unclear.

note: Kuruntokai 382: the friend says the rain that opened the mullai is untimely, for if this were the season he would have come; 118: the heroine says the forest has kept its season and rejects the friend's 'it is not the season'.
teaches: The Kuruntokai gives the friend's argument from his absence to the season's falseness, and 118 gives the heroine's refusal of it from the forest's evidence, so read together they show the untimely-rain consolation as one move in a dispute the heroine could win.

note: Kar Narpathu 11: the kodal putting out clusters like snakes' raised heads announces his swift return; 119: the kodal has gone from ladle to snake's hood to finger, bangle and parasol and has withered.
teaches: Kar Narpathu stops the kodal at its snake-hood stage, where it is a promise, while 119 follows the same flower to its withering, so together they turn the glory lily into a clock whose hood marks the hope and whose wilting marks the broken word.

note: Kural 1225: the parted woman asks what enmity she did to evening; 121: she says not one foe but many, the anril, the evening, the rain, the flute, the sea and the dark cloud, have made her their living.
teaches: The Kural names evening as the single enemy of the parted woman, and the quatrain multiplies the enemies across landscapes, showing that the evening of the Kural was the type of a whole hostile world of sights and sounds, each taking its share of her.

note: Kar Narpathu 14: the cool cloud laughs softly as the mullai shows its teeth, and the friend is sure he will come; 122: the sky seems to laugh with its lightning and the heroine's shameless life breaks.
teaches: The laughing sky is a good omen in the friend's mouth and mockery in the heroine's, which shows that the same rain-cloud laughter could be heard as welcome or as scorn and that the stock image carried no fixed meaning apart from the speaker.

note: Kural 319: harm done to others in the forenoon returns of itself in the afternoon; 123: what is done in this life bears fruit in this life, as the women who tormented us have now been burned.
teaches: The Kural's impersonal rule that harm returns soon is here voiced by an injured wife about her rivals, showing how the ethical maxim of quick retribution was taken into akam as a scorned woman's satisfaction rather than a warning to oneself.

note: Naladiyar 85 says men who forced themselves on other men's wives in a former birth are born eunuchs in this one; 123 says those who think deeds bear fruit in the next birth do not understand, since the fruit comes here.
teaches: The Naladiyar defers the reckoning to a later birth while the quatrain insists on this one, so the pair shows a live disagreement in the didactic age about where retribution is seen, with the love poet choosing the visible, present punishment.

note: Ainkurunuru 66: the wife asks who the woman is who snatched away his coming home to his rich house when he was thinking of his toddling son with his little chariot (தேரொடு தளர்நடைப் புதல்வனை). Thinaimalai 124: before the boy appears drawing his toy chariot this way, the man has already bathed and embraced her 'sisters'.
teaches: Ainkurunuru 66 grants that the toddler with his chariot did pull the father toward home and blames a rival for stopping him, while the venba times the man's straying 'before the boy appears' and so denies the child ever had that pull, which shows the toy-chariot son working as the conventional test of a straying father's heart, passed in one poem and failed in the other.

note: Ainkurunuru 403: watching the boy, who bears his grandfather's name, pull his little chariot with tottering steps, the man's heart grows great toward the son as well as the wife. Thinaimalai 139: the wife names the field town only as the town of the father of the boy whose chariot does not run (ஊராத்தேரான் தந்தை). On the reading that 139 speaks during the man's absence, the two claim opposite effects for the same sight.
teaches: In the mullai poem the son's toy chariot binds the father to the house, while the marutham wife uses the same child to name a man who is not there, so the pair shows the son as the household's strongest tie and, when that tie fails, the wife's way of addressing the father without speaking to him.

note: Kalittokai 81: the boy moves his toy chariot by hand in the yard (கால் வல் தேர் கையின் இயக்க), the father is caught coming from another woman, and the wife ends by going to the boy like a cow to the place where its calf is tied (கன்று யாத்த உழிச் செல்லும் ஆ போல்). Thinaimalai 138: in this boy's father's town the buffalo's milk runs as she thinks of her calf.
teaches: Kalittokai 81 gives the cow's pull to its calf to the mother as an open simile, while Thinaimalai 138 leaves the same yearning beast unglossed in the father's own fields, so the pair shows how the marutham poets could turn one image of parental pull from praise of the mother into a silent reproach of the father.
audit_text_issue: line 1 reported missing from the site text

note: Ainkurunuru 43: the woman tells the man of the rich town that his bard is a greater liar than he and swears many oaths (பாணன் பொய்யன் பல்சூ ளினனே). Thinaimalai 131: she tells the bard, whose lute is bent like a prawn, not to fashion words of reconciliation, since she has heard the man's lies (ஊரன்பொய்).
teaches: Ainkurunuru 43 ranks the bard's lying above the man's in a single comparison, while Thinaimalai 131 dates her refusal from the day she heard the man's own lie and so sets the bard's words aside as useless rather than worse, which shows the go-between's credit in marutham falling with his master's and not on its own.

note: Kural 801 defines old friendship (பழைமை) as friendship that does not cut down the liberties of intimacy (கிழமை). Thinaimalai 134 uses both words (கிழமை, பழமை) as two alternative reasons why she, the humble one, received the man's grace when the many women he took did not.
teaches: The Kural states as a definition that old intimacy survives the liberties a friend takes, while the wife applies the same two terms to a husband who has taken many women and cannot decide whether his return came from enduring character or from reckoning the use of old ties, so the pair shows the friendship ethic carried into marriage and the doubt it leaves when the one taking liberties is the stronger party.
audit_text_issue: 134.3-4 'கிழமை குடிநாய்கர் ... கேளா அடியேன் பெற்றா அருள்' is obscure and may be corrupt

note: Ainkurunuru 65: the wife tells the lord not to embrace her body that has borne a son, since it would spoil his chest. Thinaimalai 152: do not embrace me; our son's wet mouth would wipe off the marks of breasts, jewels and leaf-paint on your chest, and my milk would spoil your garland.
teaches: The Ainkurunuru's mother refuses the embrace by pretending to protect his chest from her post-partum body; the Thinaimalai keeps that pretext and names what is on the chest, another woman's marks, so the pairing shows the old formula of 'spoiling' was an accusation waiting to be made explicit.

note: Akananuru 26: the wife recalls that lately her husband held back from embracing her for fear of spilling the milk meant for their son. Thinaimalai 152: the wife herself refuses his embrace, saying her milk would spoil his garland.
teaches: In the Akananuru it is the husband who fears the milk and the wife who is hurt by his caution; in the Thinaimalai the wife takes up the same fear as her weapon, so together they show the nursing mother's milk standing on either side of the quarrel, as his excuse or as her refusal.

note: Kural 1311: all women feast on you in common with their eyes, philanderer; I will not come near your chest. Thinaimalai 152: the wife refuses her husband's marked chest under cover of the son's drool and her milk.
teaches: The Kural's wife refuses the chest openly and for the least offence, being looked at; the Thinaimalai's wife has proof printed on the chest and still refuses only by indirection, so the couplet's open charge and the quatrain's domestic pretext mark two registers of one refusal, the second keeping the house's peace while making the charge.

note: Kural 1306: without துனி and புலவி, love is like over-ripe and unripe fruit. Thinaimalai 153: in துனி, புலவி and ஊடல், and in the கனி union after, her eyes never see the lord.
teaches: The Kural justifies the graded quarrel as what keeps love ripe, while the Thinaimalai uses the same three words from inside the cycle and finds that none of its stages, quarrel or ripe union, lets her look at him, so the pair sets the doctrine of the quarrel as seasoning against its cost to the one who lives it.

note: Kural 1285: as the eye does not see the brush that lines it, I do not see his fault when I see him. Thinaimalai 153: my eyes never see the lord, in sulk, in union, or when he leaves in anger.
teaches: The Kural finds one moment when the eye cannot see, nearness blinding it to his fault; the Thinaimalai extends that blindness to every phase of the marutham quarrel and to the man himself, so the couplet's single paradox becomes a whole cycle in which closeness and distance alike keep him out of view.
audit_text_issue: thinaimalai_nootraimpathu:153 line 1 has a bracketed restoration (நோக்கு(எ)ன்) and the object of காணேன் is uncertain | Thinaimalai 153 line 1 (நோக்கு(எ)ன் தொடர்ந்த) and the construal of காணேன் / காணா are uncertain; the marker flagged the sense.

note: Natrinai 250: the man, come home with his son, tells the bard how his wife, seeing him approach, shrank away like a startled doe asking 'who are you?'. Thinaimalai 145: amid songs, tunes and horns he came carrying his son to our place like Indra.
teaches: The Thinaimalai gives the son-bearing return from outside, as a procession fit for Indra, and the Natrinai gives it from the man's side, where the same entry ends in his wife's recoil, so together they show that the son as passport was a public spectacle whose private outcome the poets left open.
audit_text_issue: Thinaimalai 145 lines 1-3 (கோட்டரவம் twice) are hard to construe; the marker flags the sense.

note: Akananuru 46: the red-eyed buffalo breaks its tether, raids the pond, scatters the fish and eats the lotus, and the friend says he has brought another woman home. Thinaimalai 147: the red-eyed black-horned buffalo plunges into the field pond and comes back crowned with lilies and kayal fish and carrying frogs.
teaches: The Akananuru states the situation the raiding buffalo stands for, while the Thinaimalai keeps only the image and adds the buffalo coming home dressed in the pond's spoils, which shows the image had become a sign of the straying husband that a later poet could leave unexplained and even play for comedy.

note: Ainkurunuru 95: the black-horned buffalo snaps its rope and grazes the long-eared paddy all morning; its lord gives her pain even by day. Thinaimalai 148: the dark-horned buffalo grazes the great field pond, then lows remembering its calf and comes home wearing paddy straw.
teaches: The Ainkurunuru's straying buffalo is left grazing, as the husband is left away, while the Thinaimalai brings the same animal home and gives the calf as the reason, so the pairing shows the marutham buffalo could carry the wife's hope as well as her complaint: the child that draws the stray back.

note: Natrinai 380: the friend refuses the bard, saying they are soiled with ghee and smoke and smell of the new-born son, no match for the decked women of his master's street. Thinaimalai 151: the wife tells the bard her son plays in the dust before this house, not as other women's do, and his master may go and play with 'our younger sisters'.
teaches: Both refuse the bard by setting the soiled household against the decked rivals, but the Natrinai turns the grime on the women of the house as mock unfitness, while the Thinaimalai turns it on the son and calls the rivals 'our younger sisters', so the same refusal could be humble or proud depending on whom the dirt is laid on.
audit_text_issue: thinaimalai_nootraimpathu:151 sense flagged uncertain by marker | Thinaimalai 151 and Natrinai 380 lines 10-11 are flagged uncertain.

note: Both are the friend forbidding the night visit by a path where elephants go; Akananuru 318 adds 'மன்றல் வேண்டினும் பெறுகுவை', you may have the wedding if you want it.
teaches: The four-line verse stops at the prohibition, and the long poem shows what the prohibition is for: shutting the night road is the friend's way of pressing for marriage, which Thinaimozhi 1 leaves unsaid.
audit_text_issue: thinaimozhi_aimpathu 1.4 'கரம்' is of uncertain sense

note: Akananuru 28 warns that the millet ears are bowing and stalks are showing, so the girl may soon be replaced at the field; Thinaimozhi 2 says the guarding of the fields has ended.
teaches: Read in order the two poems give the harvest as the clock of the secret love, a warning while the ears ripen and the closed field once they are cut, so the end of the field-watch is the end of their meetings.
audit_text_issue: Thinaimozhi 2 line 3 வரிஅரிதாங் is likely a corrupt வரவு அரிதாம்.

note: In Akananuru 28 the mother would replace the girl at the field if she failed to scare the parrots; in Thinaimozhi 10 the mother bars her from the field because she has learnt of the union.
teaches: The pair shows two routes to the same confinement, neglect of the field-watch and the mother's knowledge, which makes clear that the millet field is the one place the girl is allowed out, and losing it is losing him.

note: Both answer the man with the same self-naming, குறவர் மகளிரேம், we are daughters of the hill folk; 6 adds that their kin would rage, 8 that no wounded tusker came this way.
teaches: The repeated formula works as a fence: in 6 it states the kin's threat outright, and in 8 the same words deflect his hunting pretext, showing that naming the tribe is itself the friend's refusal.
audit_text_issue: Thinaimozhi 6 line 3 stray mark removed.

note: Akananuru 82 makes the hill a stage where the waterfall is the drum, the bamboo wind the flute and the bees the lute, with a peacock dancing; Thinaimozhi 7 compresses it to one line, the cascade sounding as lute, flute and drum.
teaches: In both the orchestra of the hill sets up an audience: in Akananuru 82 many saw him at the field, and in Thinaimozhi 7 the night visit will be known to the whole town, so the stage image carries the danger of the love being seen and heard.

note: Thinaimozhi 7 uses ஊரறி கௌவை, gossip the town knows, as the harm that a night visit will bring; Kural 1143 has the man welcome the ஊரறிந்த கெளவை as a foretaste of having her. On a plain reading the town's gossip is a threat in one and a gain in the other.
teaches: The same phrase is a warning in the friend's mouth and a prize in the lover's, so the Kural's couplet reads as his reply to exactly the argument the friend uses to keep him away.

note: In Akananuru 388 the young hunter asks the girls on the millet platform whether a tusker wounded by his arrow has passed by their field; in Thinaimozhi 8 the friend answers that no bleeding tusker came this way.
teaches: The long poem gives the pretext question and the short one gives only the reply, which a reader can only read as a reply because the question is a fixed form; together they show the wounded-elephant question as a standard opening the girls know how to parry.

note: Both are the woman saying that his coming will take the pallor from her shoulders: Kural 1265, after she has seen her husband with full eyes; Thinaimozhi 9, if the hill lord comes in this vengai evening.
teaches: The Kural states the cure as a rule in the wife's mouth, while the earlier stage in Thinaimozhi ties it to the flowering vengai, the season sign of weddings, so the coming that cures the pallor is, before marriage, the wedding itself.
audit_text_issue: Line 2 has தோழ!, probably தோழி with a dropped vowel sign.

note: Kural 1151, the friend (for Parimelazhagar) to the departing man: tell me if you are not going; tell your quick return to those still alive then. Thinaimozhi 12, the friend to the man leaving for wealth: who can know her helplessness better than you?
teaches: Holding them together shows two moves in the friend's attempt to stop the journey: the couplet threatens with the woman's death, while the venba appeals to the man's own knowledge of her, making him the witness who cannot claim ignorance.

note: Akananuru 229: the girl answers her friend that the man who promised to come at once has not come even in young spring, when the koel calls on the budding branch. Thinaimozhi 13: the flowering season has come and the koel has made all his sworn words false.
teaches: The Akananuru lets the koel mark the date the promise failed, while the venba makes the koel the agent that turns his oath into a lie, so the four-line form compresses the long poem's reasoning into a single accusation aimed at the bird instead of the man.

note: Kural 1264: thinking of the return of the man who left the love they shared, her heart climbs up as on branches. Thinaimozhi 14: though he left for wealth even after seeing the koel's season, her heart watches for his coming.
teaches: The couplet's heart rising in hope of his return gains in the venba a bitter premise, that he chose to leave in the very season of love, so the longing is shown to persist against her knowledge of his choice, not out of ignorance of it.

note: Akananuru 375: the girl tells her friend her eyes would not weep if she knew the man who crossed the wasteland of killers would return unharmed. Thinaimozhi 15: she asks her friend whether the man who gave up grace for wealth halts on the long waste where the hawk attacks the dove.
teaches: In Akananuru 375 fear for his safety is the whole cause of her tears, but the venba puts that fear in the same sentence as the charge that he abandoned grace, showing that the heroine's worry for him survives her own accusation against him.

note: Natrinai 9: the eloping man tells the white-toothed girl to go without strain, lingering at every shade, since the road they take (யாம் செல்லும் ஆறே) runs through cool groves where the koel calls. Thinaimozhi 16: he tells the girl with budding teeth that the place they go (நாம் செல்லும் இடம்) is to be desired, as maraa blooms and bees hum.
teaches: Both men answer the girl's fear of the waste by describing its blossoms, which shows a fixed speech of the eloping lover; the venba's own turn is to have the bees hum the paalai melody, turning the name of the dreaded land into the music that leads her across it.

note: Akananuru 355: in spring bees hum on the budding branches like the strings of a paalai lute touched by a master, the season in which the heroine fears her man's going. Thinaimozhi 16: bees hum the paalai melody as the man leads the girl away.
teaches: The same sound of bees playing the paalai mode marks the spring of a parting in the Akananuru and the spring of an elopement in the venba, so the image does not carry a fixed mood but takes its grief or its promise from the uri it serves.

note: Kural 872: take on the enmity of ploughmen whose plough is the bow rather than of those whose plough is the word. Thinaimozhi 17: the woman fears for her man passing the hamlets of those who live by ploughing with the bow, while her shoulders slacken because he left without grace.
teaches: The Kural ranks the bow-ploughmen as the lesser enemy, and the venba agrees in its own way: the bowmen are only a feared danger on his road, while the wound she actually bears, slackened shoulders, comes from his word, the promise and grace he withheld.

note: Akananuru 185: her bright bangles slip as the man crosses summer hills where seed-bearing bamboo bursts with the twang of warriors' bows. Thinaimozhi 18: on the road where sun-split bamboo sheds pearls, her bangles seem ready to fall.
teaches: In the Akananuru the bursting bamboo is a sound of violence on his road, while the venba makes the same bursting shed pearls, a treasure dropped in the land where he seeks wealth, set against her bangles falling for nothing, so the image of the split bamboo is turned from danger to the waste of what is precious.
audit_text_issue: Thinaimozhi 18 line 3 (எதிர்வன போல்இலவே) is hard to construe.

note: Kural 1234: with her partner gone her shoulders lose their old beauty and fullness and the bangles slip. Thinaimozhi 19: the woman, picturing him halting in the stony waste where the doe cries with the stag, says her shoulders slip with her bangles.
teaches: The couplet gives the wasting shoulders as the plain sign of absence, and the venba supplies what she is thinking of while they waste: his fear on the road and the paired deer that keep together, so the symptom is tied to an imagined scene rather than to absence alone.

note: Natrinai 279: the mother asks whether the feet of her jewelled girl, her anklets removed, are weary on the sun-glittering track. Thinaimozhi 20: the mother asks a man on the road whether her daughter can bear to walk the harsh waste with a youth whose bow is like Death.
teaches: Natrinai's mother fears only the road and the girl's tender feet, but the venba's mother fears the companion too, calling him Death-like, which shows the mother's grief can doubt the very youth the girl trusted for protection.

note: Kar Narpathu 8: the woodland where the kaayaa opens buds as if dipped in the collyrium of an eye announces the return of the man who went for fame. Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 21: with the collyrium-dark kaayaa in bloom, the lover has come.
teaches: The same collyrium-blue kaayaa that in the Kar Narpathu is still only a herald of the man becomes, in the Thinaimozhi verse, the flower already open when he arrives, so the mullai venbas use one stock blossom to mark both the promise and its keeping.
audit_text_issue: Kar Narpathu 8 line 2 வால்கூறும் is probably a misprint for வரல் கூறும்.

note: Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 22: the friend asks what will become of the pallor now that the rain says he will come. Kural 1265: the woman says the pallor of her shoulders will leave only after she has seen her husband with full eyes; on a plain reading they disagree on whether news of his return can touch the pallor.
teaches: The friend treats the pallor as already beaten by the season's promise, while the couplet's woman refuses any cure short of seeing him, so the couplet sounds like the heroine's unspoken reply to the friend's teasing question.

note: Both liken the thundering rain to the drums of kings (வேந்தர் ... முரசின்). Kuruntokai 380: the friend says their lover is in a far country, not before them; how shall they bear it? Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 23: the friend says he who went will come, and the rain will be greater tomorrow.
teaches: One image, the sky beating like a king's drum, serves the friend once as proof that he is coming and once as a measure of how far away he still is, which shows that in the rains the friend's comfort is a choice of reading, not a fact the season settles.

note: Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 24: the friend rests her comfort on the man who swore an oath (வஞ்சினம்) and held to it, with the rain as his token. Kural 1154: if he who said 'fear not' leaves, is there any fault in those who trusted his assuring word?
teaches: The friend builds her comfort on his oath, while the couplet asks who is to blame if such an oath fails, so together they show that the whole mullai argument of waiting rests on trusting a man's word, and the Kural names the risk the friend leaves unsaid.

note: Akananuru 74: the heroine says she could hold firm on the friend's repeated comfort (he will see the doe with the stag in the rain-fresh scrub, think of you and come today, இன்றே வருவர்) if only the herdsmen's harsh little flute did not torment her at evening. Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 25: the friend points to the buck leaping with his doe and says he will come right now (இன்னே வருவர்).
teaches: The Thinaimozhi verse gives the friend's argument by itself, and the Akananuru heroine quotes that same argument and tells us where it breaks, at evening with the flute, so the four-line comfort is shown as one turn of a longer exchange in which it does not fully hold.

note: Kuruntokai 21: though the forest's konrai says it is the rainy season, the heroine will not believe it, for he does not lie. Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 26: the friend says the thundering rain is the time he named, fitting his word.
teaches: Both trust the man's word, but they draw opposite conclusions from it: the friend reads the rain as his promise kept, the Kuruntokai woman reads his absence as proof the rain is not yet the true season, so the same faith can either confirm the season or deny it.

note: Both name the bewildering evening (மருண்மாலை, மருள்மாலை). Kural 1222: the woman asks the sad-eyed evening whether its partner is as hard-hearted as hers. Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 27: the friend calls the darkening rainy evening the sign the man set for his return.
teaches: The same evening the Kural's woman mourns as a fellow sufferer abandoned like herself is presented by the friend as the very token of his return, which shows that the evening's meaning in love poetry depends on who is speaking and whether she still trusts him.

note: Both have the thunder (ஏறு) make the gem-bearing serpent cower (மணி நாகம் அனுங்க) as the rain-cloud goes. Kar Narpathu 20: the returning man tells his charioteer the king's work is done. Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 28: the friend tells the heroine the beauty spots will spread on her breasts.
teaches: A near-identical half-line serves at both ends of the journey, in the returning man's mouth and in the waiting woman's friend's, which shows the serpent cowering at the thunder as a shared formula of the mullai rains rather than one poet's image.

note: Akananuru 14: in the evening when good cows with swollen udders ooze sweet milk (தீம்பால் பிலிற்ற) and call to their calves, the wife asks the bard how she will be at dawn if he does not remember them; the bard then sees the chariot coming. Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 30: with the herds oozing sweet milk (தீம்பால் பிலிற்ற), the friend asks 'will our man come?'
teaches: The same phrase of cows streaming milk carries the question of his return in both poems, and the long Akananuru supplies the answer the venba leaves open, the chariot on the road, so the milk-heavy herd going home is a fixed cue that the man too must be on his way.

note: Kalittokai 25 likens the woman's eyes, bangles and brow, bright while he is near and failing when he leaves, to the bond of base men who praise to the face and slander behind; Thinaimozhi 33 likens the man himself, who ate her youth and moved on, to the friendship of the base.
teaches: Both poems borrow the moral figure of the false friend for a husband's desertion, but the Kalittokai sets it on the wife's changing body while the venba sets it squarely on the man, so the same ethical simile can either describe the damage or name the culprit.

note: Kural 812 asks what it matters whether one gains or loses the friendship of those who are friends while there is profit and leave when there is none; Thinaimozhi 33 calls the husband's conduct exactly such a friendship.
teaches: The Kural can shrug at the self-serving friend because a friend can be dropped, but the wife cannot treat a husband with that indifference, since what he consumed was her youth, so the akam poem shows where the maxim's calm stops working.

note: In Natrinai 200 the friend, with the bard listening, has the potter cry through the town that women should guard against this bard's lie-wrapped crooked words; in Thinaimozhi 34 the bard is found standing in the other women's street for his own gain.
teaches: Read together the two show the bard's double standing in marutham: the man's envoy at the wife's door is, to the town and the wife, a known agent of his affairs elsewhere, and the venba adds that he profits from it.

note: Kalittokai 74 opens with a striped bee that has fed on pond flowers and backwater neythal moving on to the field lotus, and says the man joins one woman at forenoon and seeks another by afternoon; Thinaimozhi 35 likens him openly to the bee that sips fresh flowers and leaves the women only their bodies.
teaches: What the Kalittokai leaves as an opening scene to be matched with the man's day, the four-line venba states as an explicit simile with its result, the emptied body, showing the hidden image of the longer poem made plain in the later form.

note: In Kural 1183 the woman says he took her grace and modesty and gave her sickness and pallor in exchange; in Thinaimozhi 36 the friend tells the man that he both gave the beauty and took it back.
teaches: The Kural's exchange is a loss suffered in separation, but the friend makes the same giving and taking an argument against the husband: since he alone gave and took, there is no one else to blame and nothing anyone can do to him, which turns the woman's lament into an accusation.

note: In Naladiyar 390 the wife tells the bard not to lie that the man will be kind, since to him she is the tip of the sugarcane, and to tell it to those who are its middle joints; in Thinaimozhi 37 she tells the bard not to keep pressing, since she never had the gracious regard 'our younger sisters' have.
teaches: The same refusal of the bard, by the same speaker, is filed by the Naladiyar under the chaste wife, so the didactic book reads her sharp tongue to the go-between as a mark of karpu, while the akam venba keeps it as wounded pride with the ironic family word for the rivals.

note: In Kalittokai 74 the wife answers the bard who praises the man as not loveless by calling the bard, the trusting women, the man and his chariot all deluded; in Thinaimozhi 38 she stops the bard's praise of the man's goodness by pointing to the loosened hair his garland lay on.
teaches: Both wives reject the bard's praise of the husband, but the Kalittokai argues the case at length while the venba answers with a single visible sign, so the shorter form shows the refusal resting on evidence rather than rebuttal.

note: Naladiyar 390 has the wife call herself the tasteless tip of the sugarcane to the lord of the town; Thinaimozhi 39 has her say she has become the chewed pith of the cane after he ate her beauty.
teaches: The marutham wife reaches for sugarcane in both books, but the Naladiyar places her at the less sweet end of a cane still whole, a matter of rank among his women, while the Thinaimozhi has the cane already chewed and spat out, so the same image measures either neglect or use and discard.

note: Kural 1078 says the worthy are of use at a word and the base, like sugarcane, only when crushed; Thinaimozhi 39 has the wife say she has become the crushed cane's refuse.
teaches: The Kural looks at crushed cane from the side of the one who extracts the juice, as a way to get use from the mean, while the akam poem speaks from the cane's side, so the same image shows that what is crushed for its sweetness is left as waste.

note: Kural 782: the friendship of the worthy grows like the waxing moon. Thinaimozhi 41: the worthy man's bond has waned since the day she saw him, and his trysts proved false; on a plain reading the heroine's case contradicts the maxim.
teaches: The heroine's question ஐயகொல் ஆன்றார் தொடர்பு tests the Kural's rule against one man and finds it failing, so the akam poem uses the ethical maxim as a weapon: either the rule is wrong or he was never one of the worthy.

note: Natrinai 11: the friend tells the heroine, wilting since the tryst he set failed (அவர் செய் குறி பிழைப்ப), to drop the resentful thought that he will not come, for his charioteer is driving along the moonlit shore sparing the crabs. Thinaimozhi 41 is that resentful thought spoken: his trysts have turned false (செய்த குறியும்பொய் யாயின).
teaches: Held together the two give the complaint and its answer in one neythal exchange: the venba lets the heroine conclude from the failed tryst that his bond is false, while the older poem shows the friend refusing that inference and offering his gentleness on the road as proof.

note: Kuruntokai 121: the heroine grants her friend that for the hill man's failure to keep the tryst (தான்குறி வாயாத் தப்பற்கு) her own shoulders have turned pale, as the branch goes down with the langur that missed its leap. Thinaimozhi 41: for the same failure she questions his nobility.
teaches: The same failed tryst draws two answers from the heroine: in the Kuruntokai she takes the fault into her own body, while the later venba turns it outward into a charge against his worth, which shows accusation as a second, sharper register of the same situation.

note: Kural 1234: with the partner gone, the shoulders lose their old beauty and fullness and the bright bangles slip. Thinaimozhi 47: the heroine asks her friend whether he has abandoned her, as pallor spreads and the bangles of her soft shoulders slip.
teaches: The couplet states the sign as a fact of separation, while the venba makes the heroine read it as a question, has he left me?, so the slipping bangle becomes the evidence by which she learns his desertion rather than its mere effect.

note: Akananuru 260 lists the signs of evening on the neythal shore (the sun dimming, herons crying, the crab slipping into its hole, the waves falling quiet) before the heroine asks what will become of her. Thinaimozhi 48 gives a chariot cutting the sand, crabs scattering and the sun hurrying away as the evening comes.
teaches: The long poem shows that the neythal evening was built as a catalogue of shore signs ending in the heroine's dread, which lets the four-line venba keep only three signs and the bare 'evening will come' and still carry that dread unstated.

note: Kural 1081: on first seeing her the man asks whether she is a goddess, a peahen or a woman, and his heart reels. Thinaimozhi 49: the man asks whether she was a peacock, a young woman or a goddess of the sea waves, and his heart aches from her eyes.
teaches: The same three-way doubt in both shows the first-sight ஐயம் was a fixed form of kalavu, and the venba adds what the couplet leaves open: a place for the seeing, the njazhal grove, and a goddess native to that place, the one who lives in the waves.

note: Akananuru 282: the father agrees to give the girl to the hill lord whose hunters bring ivory, gold, gems and pearls together, and the household prays for the wedding day. Thinaimozhi 50: the heroine asks whether the sea lord will come to the front yard where coral, pearls and crystal are heaped as if in praise.
teaches: Akananuru 282 makes the suitor's treasure of the land the very thing that wins the father's consent, so beside it the shore's coral, pearls and crystal piled at the heroine's door read as the bride-wealth her question 'will he come?' is waiting for.
